covenants.name: Wormhout
covenants.summary: A covenant of the Normandy Tribunal, in a forest outside the town of the same name.
covenants.secrets:
The book sets it in the Normandy Tribunal (p. 77). This pack holds no Tribunal, so it stands on no roster here. Its magi, each gauntleted some 60 to 70 years ago, are given only brief statistics; the book suggests about 1200 xp in Arts and 120 in Abilities for a storyguide who fleshes them out (p. 78).

Four members, most in middle age, none near final Twilight. It was built on its founders' cooperation, and its vis sources and its mundane and magical security are excellent (p. 79).

Founded in 886 with Vindolanda's sponsorship, and bound to it by a treaty with no time limit, invoked by agreed tokens (pp. 77, 80). Vindolanda was reported destroyed 331 years before the saga opens.

The book's saga opens here: the new magi are lodged and fed and given some study time in exchange for scribing, and are waiting for an invitation from any covenant at all (p. 77). Vera and Iphimedeia are away on an investigation when Donncadh arrives (p. 80). Magi who refuse the mission are told to leave. Markus and Cornelius offer two seasons of study rights for it and may be pressed to four.

After the first adventure Iphimedeia investigates Vindolanda's survival, is reassured, and agrees to register it in the Normandy Tribunal; Wormhout honours its debt and stays an ally. Its library is open to the magi at its standard fee of 2 pawns of vis a season (p. 75). The book leaves the library's contents to the storyguide.

covenants.secrets:
Its symbol is a red griffon with claws raised, on a white field. Founded in 816. Its members: Victor filius Pralix, a leading figure of House Ex Miscellanea, now possessing the body of Brighde; Ealasaid filia Morwena, died 889; Macomb filius Ealasaid, died 889; Liam the Shapeless, filius of Brude, disappeared 889; and Iain the Unbowed, filius Liam. All followed Ex Miscellanea (p. 88). The book's list styles Victor founder of the House, a title only: Pralix founded it (p. 71).

The players hold only Scartaris at first. Victor stays Disceptator but leaves the daily running to Iain, who gives funds and advice; Victor calls dreamscape councils only when he must, since holding Hetep takes most of his attention (p. 87).

The oath gives up every tie to another covenant for lasting loyalty to this one, and binds each member to its Charter, its council and its fellow members' lives, and to fight Damhan-Allaidh and his servants until nothing of him or his work is left. By the Charter all property serves the covenant. The Disceptator is elected by the members and holds office until death or final Twilight, breaks ties and may delegate. The Council is all the members, meeting around solstices and equinoxes, or in an emergency at the Disceptator's call. Each member owes seven seasons of covenant work a Tribunal period unpaid, and further work earns three pawns a season; work is set by Petition to the Council. An expelled magus must leave within a day (p. 85).

neighbours.name: Iceland
neighbours.summary:
A rugged island larger than Ireland, and mostly unfit to live on: over half of it stands above 400 metres, high indeed so far north. Quick rivers run through lowland meadows over great waterfalls, and shift their courses from one generation to the next. Gorges slash the open plains and defeat the traveller. Pits of boiling mud, hot pools and geysers are everywhere, in over 250 hot districts with 780 springs, and old lava and ash are never far off. The highlands, with their burning ranges and vast glaciers, are left to trolls, giants, the mad and the desperate.

It rains, sleets, snows or drizzles most days, though winters are mild and a shower often gives way to a sunny afternoon. Gales and fog can make life miserable. The north is the sunniest coast and the east the warmest. The interior has clearer skies, but blizzards in every season and icy sandstorms that rise from nothing.

The land, about 800 and about 1220, as a share of the whole:
Cultivated: none, 1%
Grassland: 40%, 30%
Lakes and rivers: 6%, 6%
Bush and forest: 25%, 1%
Lava fields: 11%, 11%
Glaciers: 11%, 11%
Sand: 4%, 4%
Other wasteland: 3%, 36%

The first settlers found dwarf willow woods, and bog and marsh along parts of the coast. Clearing for firewood and pasture let the soil wash away, and the highland erosion goes on; another 8% of the grass will be lost in years to come. Ireland, by comparison, is 13% tilled, 68% grass and 5% woods.

Only the arctic fox and the polar bear are native. The bears were killed or caught and sold abroad, and one that drifts over from Greenland on the ice is soon hunted down; the foxes, as disliked, hid better. Common and grey seals feed on the coastal shelves and are hunted by orca, other whales are often seen, and walrus bask on the floes between dives for clams.

Gulls, cormorants and great auks fill the coasts, with ducks, whooping swans, owls, divers, gyrfalcons and the snow-white arctic eagle, the grandest of all. Eels, salmon, trout and Arctic char swim the rivers, and the sea is thick with food.

The settlers brought chickens, cattle, cats, dogs, sheep, goats, pigs and horses, and without meaning to, mice and rats. Goats and pigs did such harm to the thin grass that by 1000 few were kept.

Before people came, the whole island lay under a magical aura, known only to dragons, giants and magical beasts, and spirits of the land warred like the fire and ice they mirrored. The prayers of Irish priests drove that power back into the geyser fields, mountains, volcanoes and glaciers.

Icelanders have no family names: each is known as the son or daughter of the father, rarely the mother, as Una Eiriksdottir or Thord Eiriksson, and a nickname may set one man apart from another, as Viga-Thord, Battle-Thord, or Thord inn audgi, Thord the Rich.
neighbours.secrets:
Auras (p. 9): the lowlands are mundane. Dominion is low and patchy: a farm beside a church may have Divine 1, seldom reaching its neighbours, and only around the cathedrals does it cover much ground. Most faerie auras of the pagan temples went with the conversion. Lowland volcanic regions often keep Magic 1 or 2; little-travelled highlands a patchy Magic 1; mountains and glaciers normally Magic 2, peaking higher at particular sites. Before the Irish priests, the aura in many places reached right into the magic realm (p. 6).

Wards (p. 9): the magicians keep wards on the interior paths that stop trolls and landvaettir of Magic Might 20 or less, and on some stretches up to 30.

The Order (p. 9): Icelandic magicians do not know of Hermetic magi, and the Order knows little of the island. Magi suspect all Nordic lands, where many blame a powerful Order of Odin for the loss of every covenant tried there, so most shun even the Scandinavian mainland and few have heard of Iceland. In 1220 it has no known Hermetic presence.

neighbours.name: Hekla
neighbours.summary:
A burning mountain of the south-west, and the lair of the dragon Pan Caudarax, first of the Guardians. In 924 he woke to find the lowlands full of men and set the volcanic spirits to shake the land. Galdramen and trollsynir tracked him here and many died before the trollsdottir Aud found his weak spot and wounded him. Each side drew back, and a truce was struck: he called off the spirits, and the Norse pay him forty horses a year.

He has cared little for humans since, and they seldom come near. Eruptions still happen, but they are not his doing.
neighbours.secrets:
Pan Caudarax came back to his lair in 108 after almost a thousand years in Flanders and made a nest for his mate's brood. The eggs were laid in 232, and he then took the mantle of Guardian from his mate. They will hatch on the day of the solar eclipse, 22 May 1248 (p. 11).

The book prints 924 here (p. 11) and 925 in its timeline (p. 17), where vitkir join the attackers.

neighbours.name: Eldborg
neighbours.summary: A great crater in the west, alone in a flat lava field not far short of the Snaefellsnes peninsula, 200 paces across and 50 deep, torn open by Pan Caudarax's wrath about 925. The way to its wide floor goes up the outer slope and down the inner. Iceland's magicians have met here since 950, in memory of the alliance that stood against him.
neighbours.secrets:
A magical site; the book prints no aura for it (pp. 17, 27, 102).

A great volcanic crater in a flat lava field, a little off the road to Snaefellsnes.

About 200 paces across and 50 deep; horses must be left and the sides climbed. Half an hour west across country from the northward path. The hreppur meets here just after the Althing. At the meeting the book describes, over three hours there arrive 11 trollsynir, 6 vitkir, 62 galdramen (11 of them schooled) and 8 Seithkona (p. 102).

neighbours.name: Odadahraun, the Lava Fields of Misdeeds
neighbours.summary:
The wild lava north of the Vatnajokull glacier, where the East, North and South Quarters meet and which none of them truly owns. Twisted spires of rock and crumbling pumice stand among sulphur springs that belch foul air, under glaciers and volcanoes.

No church has ever touched it. Only the most desperate outlaws brave its freezing winds and scalding steam, and they are dangerous men. Unfriendly spirits of every sort haunt it, some of Pan Caudarax's older brood have settled here, and giants are fairly common, above all of the clans of Geirrod and Bergelmir.
neighbours.secrets:
Vis (p. 14): this may be Iceland's richest ground for it. A season of searching yields one pawn for each ten points of Per + Intellego + Vim + 10, likely of Perdo, Ignem, Terram, Aquam or Auram. The season costs at least a penalty to the aging roll, of a size the book does not print, and always draws the notice of something living here.

The Dominion has never reached it. The book prints no aura for it (p. 14).

neighbours.summary:
The assembly field beside a lake in the south-west, also called Thingvellir.

A place of great natural beauty with a large lake, where the river Axe runs through ravines and lava plains. For a fortnight each summer it holds the Althing and becomes the nearest thing Iceland has to a town: hundreds come, and with them traders, peddlers, brewers and people seeking a husband or a wife. Friendships and alliances are made and broken, stories told, news swapped and business done.

The richer families keep turf booths here, roofed with homespun only while the meeting lasts; the rest pitch tents. There is a local church, where the bishops lead masses on the Althing's first Sunday (LFI p. 35).

neighbours.name: Greenland
neighbours.summary:
The land Eirik the Red found in 982, once outlawed from Iceland as he had been from Norway. A Norwegian called Gunnbjorn had sighted it some fifty years earlier. Eirik found open grass and plenty of bears, foxes, caribou, sea mammals, birds and fish, spent three years marking out farms along the coast, and settlers followed in 986.

It sends out furs and hides, ropes and cables, oil, woollens and sea-ivory, white bears and falcons, and takes in corn, iron, timber, clothes and luxuries.

neighbours.name: The Eastern Settlement
neighbours.summary: The Greenland colony, governed on the Icelandic model. At its height it held 190 farms, twelve parish churches, a cathedral, a monastery and a nunnery.

neighbours.name: Helluland
neighbours.summary: Flatstone Land, which Leif Eiriksson found: mountains and glaciers, barren and without grass.
neighbours.secrets: A realm ruled by giants, where King Dumb reigned and Bard Snaefellsass was born (p. 141). Fleeing trollsynir and giants make for it in the Icelandic Wars (Icelandic Wars p. 13).

neighbours.name: Markland
neighbours.summary: Leif Eiriksson's flat forest land, with long white sands and gently shelving beaches. Greenlanders still sail there in 1220 for furs and timber.

neighbours.name: Vinland
neighbours.summary:
Wineland, rich and fertile, with mild winters. A colonist blown off course saw it first, and fifteen years on Leif Eiriksson wintered there. His brother Thorvald died by a native arrow on the next voyage.

Thorfinn Karlsefni brought three ships, 160 men, some wives and livestock, and stayed three winters before raids and quarrels over women sent him home. Freydis Eiriksdottir's attempt in 1019 turned to war at once against far greater numbers and was the last.

neighbours.name: The Guardians of Iceland
neighbours.summary:
Four great powers who answer the landvaettir, the spirits of the land, when danger comes to the island's shores. No one knows who set them there, but they are very old. The host goes first to the First Guardian, and passes to the next if he fails.

Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla tells how a warlock of King Harald of Denmark swam to Iceland as a whale. A dragon with serpents and toads drove him from the east, an eagle with its birds from the north, a gray bull with land spirits from the west, and a giant with an iron staff, leading other giants, from the south. He swam home, and the Danish fleet turned back.

The First Guardian is the dragon Pan Caudarax, whose host of serpents, toads and fishes rolls with poison vapour. The Second is Vindsvall, an eagle whom most see as a dark storm cloud: his wings are the wind, and his cry the lightning. His host is birds of every kind.

The Third is a gray bull, an aurochs as big as a house, its hide proof against iron. In 1105 it strayed after the bishop's cows at Skalholt, stayed too long and shrank, and herdsmen caught it. It has fathered strong calves; as it ages and dies a gray bull calf takes up its spirit.

The Fourth is the chief of Iceland's jotunn, an office passed on to each new chief. Bard Dumbson is the second to hold it. All the clans of giants set aside their rivalries to march with him.
neighbours.secrets:
Rules (p. 7): the landvaettir alert the Guardians only to a being of substantial magical power who means harm to the land or its people, judged as Sight of the Transparent Motive at Penetration 45, resistance counting as hostile.

Their weakness is within: they were set against invaders, and ignore magicians native to Iceland. In the Toframanna Saga the portal to the Scartaris Sanctum, opening inside Iceland, does not alert them either.

Those without Second Sight see neither the spirit hosts nor the eagle, only a tumult of air or a storm. Under the Dominion the Gray Bull's power lies dormant, so the host goes past it to the Fourth Guardian; if it were freed its host would take the shapes of land animals. The landvaettir lend the giants power (p. 7).

The landvaettir are described on p. 32, and Pan Caudarax's stats are on p. 140.

neighbours.name: The Icelandic Freestate
neighbours.summary:
Irish priests came in coracles about 790 and for eighty years spent their summers here in prayer. When the Norse arrived, they had seen enough of Vikings at home and sailed away.

Word of the island spread after Naddoddur found it in 850, just as Harald Fairhair was making himself overlord of Norway, and many had reason to leave. Within sixty years the farmland was taken, by ten to twenty thousand people from Norway and the Norse colonies of Ireland, Scotland and the Hebrides. Gaelic wives, followers and slaves came with them, but left only a few place-names and their blood.

Richer settlers raised temples and gave oxen and horses for sacrifice, and so became godar (singular godi), godly ones. A godi's power rested on how many householders, baendur (singular bondi), would freely ally with him as thingmen.

Slaves cost more to feed than they earned, and spare land had to be defended, so owners freed them as labourers and tenants. Freedmen often came to own land, and their children were born free. Most slaves were free by the tenth century, and household slaves were very rare by the mid twelfth.

Disputes first went to district spring assemblies, the varthing, each run by three local godar. With settlers from everywhere and no shared law, and no wish to ask Norway's king, the chieftains sent Ulfjot of Lon to study the Gulathing Law. With his uncle Thorleif the Wise he adapted it, and in 930 the Althing met.

Magicians came with the settlers, drawn by the island's strong spirits and plentiful magical resources, and they were busy, for with the priests gone violent spirits, trolls and beasts fell on the farms, and wards were much sought after.

Magicians were respected in pagan days, but magic in matters of honour was hated, and they kept out of feuds. A godi who practised invited talk of dishonour, so most godar chose politics, though they might seek magical help in secret. To keep the godar from leaning on them, the leading magicians formed a hreppur, which set wards against trolls on the trails, fixed the cost of their services, refused the blacklisted, backed members under pressure, treated with giants and dragons, and ruled the gathering of Ond, which is vis, from magical sites.

After the conversion of 1000 the fear of hell became real to the magicians, and from 1020 private pagan worship was banned. Within a generation vitkir went from honoured priests to likely outlaws. Other magicians worked on in the open until, in 1031, a curse helped to kill the heroic outlaw Grettir. The outrage brought a ban on all magic, with lesser outlawry for spells and full outlawry for sorcery that sickened or killed.

After a run of convictions the leading magicians met, admitted volur and visindamen to the hreppur for the first time, and gave the Christian party what it asked for. For ten years no magic was worked. Famine came, cattle sickened, fish failed, storms came unwarned, the trail wards failed and trolls took travellers and herds. In the end great baendur and godar quietly promised that cases over harmless magic would be crushed and charges of black sorcery fairly heard. The magicians came back, known to all and spoken of by none.

In the twelfth century the most successful godar began to act as aristocrats, and saw what several chieftaincies (godord) could do for a man. Around 1200 the sons of Sturla began gathering them in the Western Quarter, and the race for mastery of Iceland began. By 1220 nearly all of it lies in eight unstable domains, riki, ruled by close relatives from five families: the storgodar, big chieftains.

Most baendur have lost their free choice of godi, and storgodar take little interest in local quarrels, so rich storbaendur, big householders, have become local advocates. Their loyalty still decides contests between storgodar, and their stout refusal of every tax keeps any one man from winning outright.

Even inside the riki the storgodar rarely own every chieftaincy. Lesser chieftains lend their godord or follow a greater man and keep control under his protection, for failing to protect one's thingmen is a great shame, and few can stand alone. Yet no godi gives up his title unless honour leaves no other way.

King Hakon of Norway now reaches for the Norse lands of the North Atlantic. His father-in-law Earl Skuli threatened Snorri Sturluson at court with a fleet. Snorri talked him out of it by offering to go home and win the chieftains over to the Crown, a cause he does not mean to champion.

Timeline:
c. 4000 BC: The civilization of the Old Ones is destroyed.
c. 2000 BC: The Egyptian cult of Thoth is at its height.
c. 500 BC: The Greek cult of Hermes is at its height.
412: The cult of Mercury is officially disbanded.
767: The Order of Hermes is founded at Durenmar.
790: Irish priests, whom the Norse will call papar, reach Iceland and make it their summer retreat.
800-1100: The Viking period.
825: The Irish monk Dicuil mentions Thule in his book on the measure of the world.
850: Naddoddur the Swede, blown off his course to the Faeroes, comes on the island and calls it Snaeland, snowland.
855: Gardar Svavarsson sails round the island and winters at Husavik on the north coast.
860: Floki Vilgerdarson brings his family to Snaeland, soon tires of it and renames it Island, ice land.
870-930: The landnam, the land-taking: 10-20 thousand Norsemen claim the farmland, and the Irish priests choose not to come back.
874: Ingolfur Arnarson makes his home at a place he names Reykjavik, smoky bay.
890-930: Harald Fairhair reigns in Norway.
910-990: The life of Egil Skallagrimson: warrior, poet, magician.
925: Pan Caudarax orders the landvaettir to clear the island of people, and volcanoes stir all over it. Trollsynir, galdramen and vitkir attack him and in the end win a truce.
930: The Althing, the general assembly, is set up with the first constitution, opening what will be called the Freestate.
930: The island is declared albyggt, fully inhabited: 40-50 thousand people, 400 named settlers with their kin, women and slaves.
950: The magicians form a hreppur to guard their interests, and meet in the Eldborg caldera, which the dragon's wrath made 25 years before, in memory of their first alliance.
965: The constitution is refined: four quarters (fjordungar), each with a court at the Althing.
970: An outlaw who kills three other outlaws earns a free pardon.
979: Harald Bluetooth Gormsson of Denmark sends a trollson to look at Iceland. The Guardians meet him, and Harald gives up his plan of invasion.
982: Outlawed from Iceland, Eirik the Red sails west and comes on Greenland.
984: The native Thorvald and the German bishop Fridrekr build the first church in Iceland. Their mission does well, but the Althing they attend mocks them.
986: Greenland is colonized.
987: Bjarni Herjolfsson catches sight of Vinland.
997: A law rules that conversion may in some cases count as a defilement of the family.
1000: The Althing makes Iceland Christian, thanks chiefly to three zealous Christian godar. They argue that two faiths under one law would split the land into two states, and pressure over trade from Denmark and Norway helps. Exposing newborns, eating horseflesh and private sacrifice to the old gods stay lawful.
1001: Leif Eiriksson goes west in search of Vinland.
1002-20: Vinland's colonies are tried, and given up by 1020 at the latest under native attacks. Gathering furs and timber there may go on into the mid fourteenth century.
1005: A fifth court is set up.
1007: Holmganga, single combat, ends as a legal way of deciding a case. The last duel recorded on the islet in the Oxara was fought by the warrior-poet Gunnlaugur Serpent-Tongue against the husband of the woman he loved.
1014-1030: Olaf Haraldson, St Olaf, reigns in Norway. A treaty of 1020 with Iceland settles the rights of each country's people in the other, and with it the last pagan practices become illegal.
1030-1118: The Fridharold, the age of peace.
1031-1041: Magic helps to kill Grettir the Strong, and laws against all magic follow. For ten years the magicians give no help at all, until the godar agree to protect in secret those accused of harmless magic.
1056: The first bishopric is founded at Skalholt in the Southern Quarter, and its bishop gains a seat in the logretta.
1056-80: Isleif Gizursson is Iceland's first native bishop.
1056-1133: The life of Saemundur Sigfusson the Wise, godi of Oddi, galdraman and bishop, whose sister Halla was a seithkona.
1096: The law of tithes comes in.
1106: A second bishopric is founded at Holar in the Northern Quarter, its bishop too sitting in the logretta. Its first, Jon the Saint Ogmundarson (1106-1121), a mighty foe of heathen ways, is later made a saint. Bergthor Hrafnsson, Haflidi Masson and others write down the laws, a work that comes to be called Gragas, Grey Goose.
1122-1133: Ari the Learned writes the Islendingabok, a history from the founding to the death of Bishop Gizur in 1118.
1123: Iceland's Christian law is set down as a code.
1218-1220: Earl Skuli, for King Hakon of Norway, makes an expedition to Iceland to secure trade. Snorri Sturluson heads off violence by agreeing to help bring Iceland under Norway.

details.decides: No king: the godar and the Althing, under the law.
details.rules: One law for the whole island, from 930. Magic of any sort is outlawed, though harmless magic goes unpunished by quiet agreement. Slavery stays lawful, but by 1220 debt slaves are the only ones often seen.

neighbours.secrets:
The law on magic is quoted from Gragas on p. 14: lesser outlawry for spells, a panel of twelve, and full outlawry for black sorcery.

Figures differ in the book: ten to twenty thousand settlers (pp. 8, 17) against 40-50 thousand people by 930 (p. 17). The hreppur is of the early tenth century on p. 12 and 950 on pp. 11 and 17. Skuli's expedition of 1218-1220 in the timeline (p. 18) sits oddly with the fleet Snorri talks him out of sending (p. 16). Both are entered as printed.

Spellings: Isleif Gizursson and Jon Ogmundarson follow p. 43, where p. 18 prints Gizarson and Ogmudarson, and Bishop Gizur follows p. 43 for Gizurr.

neighbours.name: The Svinfellingar
neighbours.summary: The first family to reach beyond one or two godord. By 1220 they own the whole Eastern Quarter, split into two riki under the brothers Orm and Thorarin Jonsson.

neighbours.name: The Asbirningar
neighbours.summary: Named for Asbjorn Arnorsson, of about 1100. Kolbeinn Tumason first ruled Skagafjord, added Hunavatnsthing, and by his death in 1208 had reached the western edge of the Northern Quarter. His brother Arnor leads them now, but is failing, and Kolbeinn the Young, Arnor's son, looks likely to follow soon.

neighbours.name: The Oddaverjar
neighbours.summary: Jon Loftsson of Oddi was so respected that chieftains of all four Quarters sought him as arbitrator. He and his sons Orm and Pall, later bishop, came to rule all of Rangarthing. Pall died in 1211 and Orm in 1218, so the chieftaincies are shared among the third son, Saemundur, and his children.

details.decides: The family rules its district as a group.

neighbours.name: The Haukdaelir
neighbours.summary: Prominent in bringing Christianity to Iceland, they hold all three chieftaincies of Arnesthing, and keep a famous school at Haukadalur.
neighbours.secrets: The history prints Haukdaelir (p. 15) and the section on literacy Haukadalja (p. 24); the pack uses the first.

neighbours.name: The Sturlungar
neighbours.summary: Descended from Sturla Thordarson of Hvamm in the Western Quarter. Sturla himself never held more than one chieftaincy, but his sons Thord, Snorri and Sighvat, each with a riki, are among the most powerful and ambitious chieftains of the age.

neighbours.name: Riki of Skaftafellsthing
neighbours.summary: A Svinfellingar domain, ruled by Orm Jonsson since 1212.

neighbours.name: Riki of Mulathing
neighbours.summary: A Svinfellingar domain, ruled by Orm's brother Thorarin Jonsson since 1220.

neighbours.name: Riki of the Asbirningar
neighbours.summary: The west of the Northern Quarter, from Skagafjord through Hunavatnsthing. Arnor is storgodi, in failing health.

neighbours.name: Riki of Rangarthing
neighbours.summary: The Oddaverjar's district, shared by Saemundur son of Jon Loftsson and his children.

neighbours.name: Riki of Arnesthing
neighbours.summary: The Haukdaelir's three chieftaincies.

neighbours.name: Riki of Snaefellsnes and Dalir
neighbours.summary: Thord Sturluson, content most of the time with one chieftaincy, shares the district with his ambitious nephew Sturla Sighvatsson, but men still count Thord the storgodi.

neighbours.name: Riki of Borgarfjord
neighbours.summary: Snorri Sturluson moved here in 1202 for his wife's inheritance, and is quickly securing other chieftaincies of the Thverarthing.

neighbours.name: Riki of Vadlathing and Thingeyjarthing
neighbours.summary: All the east of the Northern Quarter. Sighvat, third son of Sturla, started in Dalir and moved north to Eyjafjordur for chieftaincies given to his son.

neighbours.name: King Hakon Hakonarson of Norway
neighbours.summary: Called the Elder, and still a youth in 1220, he seeks control of every Norse land in the North Atlantic. Earl Skuli Bardson, his father-in-law, acts for him.

neighbours.name: The Storgodar
neighbours.summary: The big chieftains, closely related men of the five great families who rule the eight riki. Local quarrels bore them, and the householders' refusal of every tax keeps each from final mastery.

details.rules: Their rise and their limits are told on pp. 15-16.

neighbours.name: The Storbaendur
neighbours.summary: The big householders, rich men who stepped in as local advocates when the storgodar lost interest in small disputes. Their loyalty still decides contests between storgodar, and fighting other men's cases brings them respect and wealth.

neighbours.name: The Draug
neighbours.summary: The restless dead of the early settlement. With no Christian burial to lay them, the magic in the air sometimes raised a corpse, which troubled its farm until magic or metal ended it. Only an enchanted burial kept a body in the ground.

neighbours.name: The Papar
neighbours.summary: The Irish priests who summered in Iceland from about 790, and whose prayers drove back the magical beasts. They fled the Norse and did not return.

neighbours.name: The Skraelingar
neighbours.summary: The people of Vinland, named screechers or uglies by the Norse. They traded gladly at first, keen on metal, which Karlsefni would not sell as weapons, and on red cloth. When the cloth ran out the raids began. With no shared tongue no peace could be made, and their numbers overwhelmed the last Norse attempt.

neighbours.name: The Storgodar Feud
neighbours.summary: Driven by the ambition of the Sturlungar and their rivals, and by the Crown of Norway waiting for them to exhaust themselves. These are the last four decades of the Freestate as the Sturlunga Saga tells them; the book points to its bibliography (p. 143) for more. The stages follow pp. 18-19.

details.antagonist: The storgodar, and King Hakon of Norway

stages.title: Snorri's second term
stages.ignored: Snorri Sturluson is Lawspeaker again until 1231. The Prose Edda is composed in 1222.

stages.title: The Snorrunga godord
stages.ignored: Snorri and Thord failed to claim their right, and Sighvat took the godord and gave it to his son Sturla. Snorri demands it at the Althing, gets no decision, and seizes it, helped by his violent brother-in-law Thorvald of Vatsfjord. That summer Thorvald is burnt to death in revenge.

stages.title: Thorvald's sons strike
stages.ignored: Blaming Sighvat and Sturla, they destroy Sturla's property while he happens to be away.

stages.title: A brief respite
stages.ignored: Snorri proves he had no part in the attack, and makes peace with his nephews and with Sighvat.

stages.title: Sturla's killing
stages.ignored: Seeking peace, Sturla is insulted by Thorvald's sons and kills them, and goes on pilgrimage to Rome for it. Snorri's illegitimate son Oraekia takes the Vatsfjord godord and sends armed bands to plunder his own people.

stages.title: The promise in Norway
stages.ignored: Coming home from Rome, Sturla falls under the sway of Hakon and Skuli, and promises to subdue Iceland for the title of earl.

stages.title: Sturla against Snorri
stages.ignored: Sturla raises an army. Snorri will not fight his kin and flees to the Eastern Quarter, though Thord tries to reconcile them. Sturla takes Rekjaholt. Oraekia harries Borgarfjord by sea, is taken by Sturla's false offer of peace, and escapes blinding and maiming. Roused, Snorri attacks and is beaten.

stages.title: The summons
stages.ignored: To end it Hakon calls the godar to Norway, and Snorri and his allies go.

stages.title: Orlygsstad
stages.ignored: Sturla rules most of Iceland, opposed only by Kolbeinn the Young and Gizur Thorvaldsson, husbands of Snorri's daughters. Sturla seizes Gizur by a trick; Kolbeinn forms a league and Gizur escapes to join it. At Orlygsstad Sighvat and Sturla are beaten. New tyrants replace the old.

stages.title: Earl Snorri
stages.ignored: Hakon's plan has failed. Duke Skuli makes Snorri an earl, to rule Iceland for Norway if Skuli takes the crown. Snorri goes home.

stages.title: Skuli's fall
stages.ignored: Skuli's bid for the throne ends in his death.

stages.title: The death of Snorri
stages.ignored: Hakon suspects Snorri and names Gizur to bring him to Norway or kill him. Warned, Snorri escapes Kolbeinn at the Althing to a church. That summer Gizur and Kolbeinn enter his home at Rekjaholt in secret and kill him. Oraekia tries to avenge him and is banished.

stages.title: The Sturlungs fade
stages.ignored: Gizur leads the south alone and Kolbeinn holds the west and north. Thord Kakali, Sighvat's only surviving son, comes home to avenge the family.

stages.title: Haugnes
stages.ignored: In the greatest battle Iceland has seen, Thord breaks Kolbeinn and his kinsman Brand and takes the north and west. He and Gizur agree to Hakon's arbitration; the next spring Hakon favours Thord, who rules unopposed for four years while Gizur stays in Norway.

stages.title: The honourable captive
stages.ignored: Hakon, jealous, keeps Thord in Norway, and sends Gizur home to win full recognition of the Crown.

stages.title: Earl Gizur
stages.ignored: Gizur is made earl over the North and South Quarters and all of Borgarfjord.

stages.title: The Old Covenant
stages.ignored: At local assemblies Hakon's men offer peace for allegiance. The men of the North and South swear, giving him suzerainty and keeping Icelandic law. Hakon abolishes every godord, and storgodar who will not swear lose their power.

stages.title: King Magnus
stages.ignored: Hakon dies. His son Magnus Law-Mender takes care not to offend the Icelanders.

neighbours.secrets: The book spells Thorvald's fjord Vatsfjord and Vatfjord, Borgarfjord also Bogarfjord, and Kolbeinn also Kolbein (pp. 15, 18-19); Skuli is Earl on p. 16 and Duke on pp. 18-19. The story here uses one spelling of each. Snorri's home is printed only as Rekjaholt.

neighbours.name: The Eclipse of 1248
neighbours.summary: The dragon's eggs, laid at Hekla in 232, are due to hatch on one day. The book says no more of what follows (p. 11).

stages.title: The eggs hatch
stages.ignored: On the day of the solar eclipse of 22 May 1248.

neighbours.name: The Fire-Giant's Illusions
neighbours.summary: A possible encounter in the Lava Fields of Misdeeds (p. 14). The characters are caught in a fire-giant's illusions.

neighbours.name: The Outlaws' Blood Bargain
neighbours.summary: A possible encounter in the Lava Fields of Misdeeds (p. 14). Outlaws here feed the blood of those they catch to spiteful spirits, and are paid for it.

details.antagonist: Outlaws, and the malicious spirits they serve

neighbours.name: The Brood's Toll
neighbours.summary: A possible encounter in the Lava Fields of Misdeeds (p. 14). A pair of Pan Caudarax's elder young stop any magus crossing the fields and make him pay in vis.

details.antagonist: Two older dragons of Pan Caudarax's brood

neighbours.name: The Icelanders
neighbours.summary:
Iceland has no towns and no villages: nearly everyone lives on a farmstead. Cattle feed the household, sheep earn its trade, and the short, thick-coated Scandinavian horse is the only other beast kept in numbers. Hay is the great crop, for the stock cannot outlast the winter without it, and a poor hay harvest means real hardship. Only the richest land of the south and west tries barley, the summers are barely long enough, and most cereal comes in by ship, so strong drink is scarce.

With trees gone and the volcanic rock too hard to dress, walls are of turf and enclosures stay small: a manured hayfield and a little special pasture before or around the house. The longhouse is turf too, long and narrow and a little broader at the middle, with its door under a small gable near one end of the front wall; grass climbs its sides until it seems part of the hill. Inside, broad benches line the walls and a long fire runs down the hall for heat and cooking, with little holes at the roof's foot for light and smoke. People sleep in the hall, the master often in a bed closet that locks. Beasts are housed apart.

Ten adults and children is the usual farm; a poor tenant has room for his family and a couple of labourers; a godi or a rich farmer has a large building of several rooms, all on one level, that sleeps twenty or thirty. Only the most prosperous have a second farmhouse, the first usually being enlarged instead.

Dress follows the mainland: a long shirt and trousers for men; for women a long shift, often pleated, under a front and back apron held by brooches below the shoulders. Cloth is the natural brown, black, grey or white of the wool. Dyed cloth shows wealth and comes out for the Althing, and the rich wear imported linen beneath.

details.rules: Farmsteads in 1220, as printed: Eastern Quarter 1260, Southern 1750, Western 1580, Northern 2140. The book totals these as 4560, though they add to 6730. Population between 60 and 70 thousand, which at ten to a farm (p. 20) fits the 6730. Pp. 20-21, 24.

neighbours.name: The Godar
neighbours.summary:
The chieftains, the island's social elite; one is a godi. Each holds at least one godord, a chieftaincy that is property in law: it can be bought, sold, inherited or held by two or more men who split its duties. By 1220 most of the forty-eight are held by just five families.

A godi is no feudal lord. He is the link between his thingmen and the law, sits on the law council (logretta) and names judges at assemblies. His thingmen often find it worth their while to bear arms for him but owe him nothing of the kind, and though a godord is no territory, men mostly choose a godi who lives close by.

details.decides: Their chieftaincies, the godord, each a legal entity within one of the thirteen districts.
details.rules: A woman may inherit a godord but not run it: she names a man to act for her, and can do well through him. Pp. 21, 23.

neighbours.name: The Baendur
neighbours.summary:
The householders; one is a bondi. The household is the root of the whole society: usually one farmstead with its fields and cattle, a husband and wife, their employees, their children and their old or infirm kin. It often fills one valley, headland or mountainside, and the place often bears its founder's name. A large farm may hold several households, sometimes under one roof, and those with shares in a property may share the title.

Every householder declares himself in thing with a godi of his own choosing. The tie is not feudal: it gives him a legal residence for the courts. Since everyone is in theory of some household, everyone belongs to a quarter and a district.

details.rules:
Owning land or milk animals makes a man a bondi; the bar is low, and a moderately prosperous tenant or hut man can form a household. A landowner must declare himself in thing even with no milk animals; a man with neither land nor milk animals belongs to the thing of the householder who takes him in (from Gragas).

Richer baendur pay thing tax. Of those who pay it, a godi may require one in nine to go with him to the Althing; the rest pay for that retinue. Paying thing tax also gives full rights to sit on legal panels (p. 34) and full membership of the local hreppur. P. 21.

neighbours.name: Tenants
neighbours.summary: Men who rent their land for a year at a time, taking it up or giving it up at the moving days. They count as baendur but may fall short of the thing tax.

details.rules: Moving days fall six weeks after the start of summer. Rent is at most a tenth of the land's value. The tenant must keep the land's value up, above all its full yield of hay. A landowner must keep a tenant who cannot feed his family until the next moving days. Pp. 21-22.

neighbours.name: Hut Men
neighbours.summary: Renters who do not farm: fishermen as a rule, or men of some other trade. Their living fails in famine even when they usually keep themselves, so they often move into the farmstead for the winter, and the landowner may ask for their labour in return.

details.rules: A landowner needs his local hreppur's leave for each hut man, so that he makes no more than he can support; without it both he and the hut man risk lesser outlawry. P. 22.

neighbours.name: Slaves
neighbours.summary: Once common, captives of Irish, Scottish or Saxon stock and their children. By 1220 a slave is a rare sight, most likely brought from the mainland, where the trade goes on. Debt-slaves also exist, usually for a time only.

neighbours.name: Freedmen
neighbours.summary: Freed slaves, who stand as dependents of their former owners under a new contract. The children of freedmen are freeborn and owe nothing.

details.rules: The former owner must support a freedman who cannot support himself, inherits from one who dies with no heirs, and takes the blood money if one is killed. P. 22.

neighbours.name: Honour among the Icelanders
neighbours.summary:
Honour stands at the centre of Icelandic life, and the coming of Christianity has not moved it: godar, priests, rich and poor all weigh a person by it first, and piety comes a distant second. Meekly offering the other cheek is a foreign idea to most.

A man's honour rests on his stock, his land and his lawsuits as much as on his weapons. A well-run farm, good marriages for his kin and skill at law all earn it. This is no knight's code: it allows for stratagem and a measure of deceit, and creeping up by night to burn a family in its house does not stain it, so long as the deed is owned.

Rank makes honour delicate. A plain farmer knows where he stands beside a chieftain, and each knows how to treat the other; where dominance or equality is open to question, offence is hard to avoid.

Icelanders prize moderation, hof: the just and temperate man tends to prosper in the sagas. Its opposite, ohof, is excess and unfair dealing that frightens enemies, allies and the man's own kin alike, and those who practise it rarely last before other leaders band against them.

details.rules:
Whoever gives, in gifts or in injury, is paid back in kind. Hiding what you have done is contemptible.

Hof and ohof: the magi of a Toframanna Saga gain greatly by showing hof and shunning ohof. Pp. 22-23.

neighbours.name: Kin, Fostering and Vinfengi
neighbours.summary:
Kin come first in any need. But the island is small and its great folk much intermarried, so a man often finds close relations on the other side of a quarrel. Help usually comes from the side of the family, from brothers and cousins, and less from uncles and nephews.

So Icelanders make kin of the spirit as well. Children are fostered in another household by agreement between the fathers. Men blend their blood in a rite to become foster-brothers, sworn brothers or oath brothers, and when vengeance is due such kin are often more to be relied on than those of blood. Vinfengi is a formal friendship that promises political and legal support, now or later.

neighbours.name: The Women of Iceland
neighbours.summary:
Icelandic women have a real say in their own lives: they may own property and lead households, and answer to outlawry for injury and killing. Much of their power is worked behind the scenes, in feuds they help end or help keep alight, shaming men into action with unpaid debts or cooling hotheads before a squabble turns to blood.

Marriage offers pass between fathers or guardians, but the woman is normally asked, and a widow may refuse. The groom pays a bride price and her family gives a dowry, both hers, and in a divorce she takes both with any increase. Some women choose instead to be a frilla, the concubine of a man of rank, as a folk saying recommends over a bad marriage; many such matches exist because kinship forbids marriage. Both divorce and the frilla survive in 1220 against Christian teaching.

details.rules: Women cannot act as advocates or sit on legal panels; a woman with a godord uses a male representative at the things. A betrothed couple must by law own at least 120 law ounces between them, perhaps twenty years' saving for a landless worker; the law means to keep children from being born destitute and is hard to enforce. P. 23.

neighbours.name: Poets and Saga-Tellers
neighbours.summary:
Weather and the long winter nights keep people indoors, and they fill the time with an occasional board game, stories and verse. Reciting sagas is a respected skill, and a traveller with many of them, well told, is welcome anywhere.

A good poet adds to his name. His verses lean on Norse myth and show his learning as well as his craft, and the great saga heroes were warrior poets, ready at any moment with something witty, flattering, insulting or obscure. A poem can win a place as a king's retainer, save a neck or start a feud. A proper Icelander facing death should find a verse or several, and a man speared through the heart may still spend his last breath on a jest.

neighbours.name: Letters and Learning
neighbours.summary:
Literacy came with Christianity. The new faith needed more teachers than it had, so many godar and baendur took orders and learned Latin and letters, or sent sons abroad who came home with Scripture, and these godi-priests founded schools that still stand in 1220. The most famous are at the homes of the Haukdaelir at Haukadalur and the Oddaverjar at Oddi.

Good Latin and letters are now common among wealthy men's sons, and authors such as Snorri Sturluson have lately begun writing verse and prose on Norse and Icelandic tradition.

neighbours.name: The School at Haukadalur
neighbours.summary: One of the two most famous schools in Iceland, kept at the home of the Haukdaelir. P. 24.

neighbours.name: Homespun and the Three Ounces
neighbours.summary:
Silver is scarce, so Icelanders trade in standard lengths of homespun, the woollen cloth they wear and sail under at home and abroad. Its quality and width are fixed: a bolt is two ells wide, and twelve ells of homespun means a sheet two ells across and twelve long.

Wool in bulk, homespun, skins and dairy goods buy the imports. White falcons, bears, sulphur and walrus ivory go abroad as well, in small amounts. Rents and debts are mostly settled with the wool and dairy work of the household.

details.rules:
An ell is about 49 cm. The law ounce, the national rate for fines, is 6 ells. The standard ounce, the district rate for trade, rent and tithes, is 4 ells. The silver ounce, the international rate, is the true weight of silver. Eight ounces of any kind make one mark of that kind.

The law council sets the law ounce's silver value each year; in 1220 it is one-sixth of a silver ounce. So a silver ounce is worth 6 law ounces, 9 standard ounces or 36 ells, and a standard ounce is worth two-thirds of a law ounce. Prices are set in standard ounces at the spring things, district by district. Pp. 24-25.

neighbours.name: Farm, Shore and Larder
neighbours.summary:
In summer the farmers of a region share common land and highland pasture. Lambs and gelded rams go up to the highest grazing, while ewes and cows stay on the lower land by the dairies. Ewes left unmilked grow more and better wool, the cash crop, so the dairies run mostly on cow's milk, making butter, cheese and above all skyr, a thick curd that keeps through winter in great wooden vats half sunk in the ground. Grazing is largely held in common; what separates one farm from another is how much hay it makes and how well its farmer judges the stock it can carry.

The commons give landless men a chance to rise. Seals are widely hunted, and a stranded whale, with its mountain of meat and blubber, can start a bitter dispute. Whale keeps fermenting in purpose-built pits. Blubber serves for frying where butter is short, for proofing leather and, from seals, for caulking boats; seal and shark oil burn in the lamps.

Trout and char run all year and salmon in season, and may be smoked. Cod dries on open racks in the arctic wind, cheap work for one fisherman, and dried and smoked fish sell in quantity at home, above all in the fasts. Most meat is boiled and steeped in vats of sour whey; this surr can be eaten from the barrel. There are sausages of meat, suet, liver and blood. Salt is short, so butter is left to ferment sour and keeps a long time. Edible lichen stands in for meal, birds and their eggs are taken, and dried dung is the ordinary fuel.

neighbours.name: Roads and Travellers
neighbours.summary:
The descendants of famous seamen now have few ships, for want of wood. Horse paths reach almost every part of the land, and goods go by the tough native packhorses over steep and stony ways.

Travellers usually sleep and eat at farms along the road. Hospitality marks an honourable man, and little is asked of a guest beyond good manners, a small gift, and his tales and gossip.

details.rules: A householder is bound by law to shelter only those on religious or legal errands, such as taking a child to baptism or going to thing for a case. Pointless wandering is illegal: an able-bodied man who does it is a tramp, and the penalty is lesser outlawry. The physically or mentally disabled are exempt, and a district usually shares their care by special arrangement. P. 26.

neighbours.name: Trade, Gifts and Raids
neighbours.summary:
Iceland has no standing marketplace. Markets gather when there is cause: the things are yearly meetings where shoemakers, swordsmiths and the like ply their crafts, each bishop's see holds a fair on certain feast days, and locals flock to a trading ship to buy its goods and deal with each other. A fishing station comes nearest to a lasting market, but sells only fish.

Prices differ from district to district, so a peddler can live by carrying goods between them and now and then saves enough for a farm of his own, but petty trading is despised and his low standing follows him. Long-distance trade is another matter: a man may buy much from a ship and sell it on at a profit with no shame, given capital and connections.

Between near equals, exchange is one more move in the game of honour. The gift is its finest form, since it leaves the receiver to choose what comes back and when. Refusing a gift, or returning one at once, may show distrust or hostility; waiting too long may show resentment; and never answering may mean utter contempt or an admission of lasting superiority, as the case may be.

A failed bargain may turn into a raid, the open taking of goods. Theft, the secret taking, is deeply dishonourable, and a serious lawsuit follows if it comes to light. A wasted journey is a bitter humiliation, and such an insult rarely goes unanswered, though most deals proposed between men of rank are well received and a trip to arrange a marriage is seldom thought hostile.

details.rules: Raiders are under forfeit immunity (p. 38): the defender may kill or hurt them without legal consequence, or may honourably stand aside and sue, so that the raider pays in the end at a price third parties set. Land, marriage and dowry deals are formalised by a witnessed handshake, the handsal. Pp. 26-27.

neighbours.name: The Hreppar
neighbours.summary:
Every farmer belongs to a hreppur, a local cooperative with fixed bounds and no tie to the godar. It insures its members and looks after the poor who have no one legally bound to keep them, meeting at least three times a year to gather and share out tithes and other gifts for the poor.

The old, the infirm and the mentally disabled are lodged with one household for a set term, then passed to another, so the burden falls on all the members by their wealth.

details.rules: A member who loses over a quarter of his herds to disease may recover half the loss, and half the value of fire damage to his home, at most three times in a lifetime. The other members fund it, each up to 1/120 of his total wealth; if that falls short, claims shrink in proportion. Full membership goes with paying thing tax (p. 21), and the hreppur licenses hut men (p. 22). The magicians keep a hreppur of their own on this model, the Galdramen Hreppur. P. 27.

neighbours.name: The Children of Ymir
neighbours.summary:
Giant and troll clans fell back to Iceland as men pressed into Scandinavia, and stayed when men followed, having nowhere further to go. They live in remote places of strong magic aura, many of them regiones or otherwise hard to reach, mostly in small families of one parent, often alone, and children.

All descend from Ymir, the first frost-giant, whom Odin and his brothers slew to make the world. From his arms came a noble brood, friendly to gods and men, the primal powers: Mimir, Odin's friend and teacher; Bestla, Odin's mother; Natt, giantess of the Night; and the three Norns. From his feet came a foul and misshapen brood, sworn enemies of gods and men, most of them drowned when Ymir's blood flooded Jotenheim at his death.

Christian Norsemen use troll and giant for the same thing. The learned draw a line: giants proper, the jotnar (one is a jotunn), are mighty in magic, often of the first brood and the true image of their race, while trolls are a fallen form, smaller, cave-dwelling, slow and man-eating, mostly of the second brood, their bodies showing how far they have sunk. The race divides into clans and families, and trolls and their ancestral clans commonly disown one another.

Some giants shelter travellers, who in such remote parts are mostly outlaws, and a number of Icelandic trollsynir (p. 51) come of bored, lonely daughters of such hosts and an occasional outlaw. Most giants have no love for humans, but few ever meet one, for men in their right minds stay out of the ice and fire where giants live.

details.rules: No more than four hundred giants in Iceland in 1220. Pp. 29-31.

neighbours.name: The Clan of Hrym
neighbours.summary: The Frost giants under Hrym, the largest clan. Frost was the power pagan Norsemen feared most and felt closest. They are implacable and tireless in their aims, often the wisest of giants, and man's greatest foes.

details.rules: Typical personality traits: Wise, Vengeful, Hateful. Pp. 30-31.

neighbours.name: The Clan of Thrym
neighbours.summary: The Noise giants or Storm giants, the gale's shriek and the thunderclap, who blast crops and waste the ground. The most violent of giants, they revel in destruction at every chance, are slow of wit and easily fooled.

details.rules: Typical personality traits: Violent, Gullible, Greedy. P. 31.

neighbours.name: The Clan of Geirrod
neighbours.summary: The Fire giants, wildfire in the woods and the lightning's stroke; the most hotheaded of giants, yet often the cleverest.

details.rules: Typical personality traits: Sly, Quick-Tempered, Meticulous. P. 31.

neighbours.name: The Clan of Gymir
neighbours.summary: The Sea giants, the whirlpool and the storm-wave. Aegir and his dreadful wife Ran, its best known, were once worshipped as gods. They are the most changeable of giants, famous for their hospitality and not at all for courage.

details.rules: Typical personality traits: Fickle, Hospitable, Cowardly. P. 31.

neighbours.name: The Clan of Bergelmir
neighbours.summary: The Rock giants, who cause avalanches and earthquakes: one of the oldest lines and the most degenerate, many having lost their magic and grown more trollish with the centuries. Often slow but brave, and proud to the point of stupidity.

details.rules: Typical personality traits: Proud, Slow Witted, Boastful. Pp. 31-32.

neighbours.name: The Children of Surt
neighbours.summary: Fire beings apart from Geirrod's clan, living in the world's hottest places, foes of gods and men, the very sign of volcanoes and lava flows. Surt, who leads them, will burn the world when Ragnarok is over.

neighbours.name: The Etin Brides
neighbours.summary: Giantesses on friendly terms with gods and men, from any of the five clans, though their brothers and sisters may hate mankind. Several Norse kings and heroes had one for a blood-mother or foster-mother.

details.rules: Likely the mothers or grandmothers of any player character trollsynir. P. 32.

neighbours.name: The Landvaettir
neighbours.summary:
Landvaettir (one is a landvaett) is the catch-all word for the host of spirits of Iceland, which swarmed with them before people came. The first Norse settlers took care to unship the dragon prows of their longships before nearing land, so as not to frighten them. When temples rose, some spirits grew close to the gods worshipped there, and so to the worshippers, and the Islendinga Saga tells of the great harm they did when Christians destroyed those temples.

There are four broad kinds: the true landvaettir, the alfar, the husvaettir and the yarthkin.

details.rules:
Landvaettir partake of both Magic and Faerie: those closest to mankind are nearest the fay, and those who kept apart as pure spirits of nature nearest the Magic Realm. For realm interaction treat them all as using Faerie power, except in magical auras, where they count as magical creatures; both sorts are therefore met in the magical auras that dot the land.

The few faerie auras are mostly heathen temple sites the Dominion has not taken, which also draw landvaettir, chiefly those who served there. All Icelandic spirits are by nature invisible and insubstantial; some can become visible, or material, not always both at once. Pp. 32-33.

neighbours.name: The True Landvaettir
neighbours.summary: Creatures of pure magic in Iceland's wildest places, the most remote and least fathomable of its spirits, capable of good and ill, and mostly happy to keep away from people. To the Second Sight they usually look like animals, the strongest like dragons and other fantastic beasts.

details.rules: They are the chief source of galdramen's magic (ch. 6). Their Might counts as ten points higher against a faerie-affecting spell. P. 33.

neighbours.name: The Fylgjur
neighbours.summary:
Spirits (one is a fylgja) that attach themselves to particular people, close kin to the old Norse idea of the soul, and passed down from an ancestor like any other trait. Most are invisible and immaterial; those who can see them speak of animal shapes and sometimes giants. A seithkona's is most often a falcon, cat or hare, the beasts of the goddess Freyja. Heroes of legend had strong ones that could appear and fight, and magicians are known for theirs.

A fylgja warns by a dream of an animal that hints at the danger, by an unseen daytime appearance in a scene that mirrors it, or by getting under its ward's feet, so that a stumble for no reason may be a warning. That is usually all it can do in the physical world.

details.rules:
Usually Magic Might about 10, with few powers and little reach into the physical world. Icelanders with the Premonitions Talent, as all galdramen have, get their premonitions from it. Premonitions is common among Icelanders, and fylgjur take special offence at malign magic on their wards or families, so such magic hardly ever passes unnoticed and unrecognised.

They count among the true landvaettir, so their Might is ten points higher against a faerie-affecting spell. Pp. 32-33.

neighbours.name: Hamingja
neighbours.summary: Fylgjur so devoted that they take human form, often giants or warrior-women.

details.rules: Best represented by the Guardian Angel or Ghostly Warder Virtue. P. 32.

neighbours.name: The Alfar
neighbours.summary: Alfar (one is an alf) are the spirits who have had most to do with people, above all in the pagan temples, and many still serve the deities they knew before Iceland turned Christian. House Merinita will find them familiar, for they are much like the sidhe. Thor, Frey, Baldur and Odin were the four best loved gods of heathen Iceland, and each has his alfar.

neighbours.name: The Alfar of Thor
neighbours.summary: Fiercely protective of people against trolls and giants. They show themselves to warn communities of raids, and may even help drive the danger off if well treated.

neighbours.name: The Alfar of Frey
neighbours.summary: Concerned with the fertility of land and livestock and the health of all living things.

neighbours.name: The Alfar of Baldur
neighbours.summary: Followers of the god of peace, the gentlest and kindest of their race, who have been known to heal those in great need.

neighbours.name: The Alfar of Odin
neighbours.summary: The most warlike of their race, bloodthirsty yet at heart benevolent, and hard for many people to deal with.

neighbours.name: The Husvaettir
neighbours.summary: House-spirits, close allies of the alfar and much like the brownies and other low faeries of the mainland. They often live in rocks near a settlement and, for gifts of food, help with chores, drive off vermin and are a blessing to the family. Slighted, they have driven families out of their homes with spite and noise.

neighbours.name: The Yarthkin
neighbours.summary: Spirits of any of the other kinds whose growing dislike of people has turned them towards malice. They are found all over Iceland, most of all near giants and trolls.

details.rules: Summoned when galdramen sing curse-songs and disease-songs. Their Might counts as ten points higher against a faerie-affecting spell. P. 33.

neighbours.name: The Tramar
neighbours.summary: Yarthkin who are spirits of evil magic.

neighbours.name: The Kveldrida
neighbours.summary: Yarthkin who are spirits of sickness, often seen as old women riding three-legged horses.

neighbours.name: A Matter of Honour
neighbours.summary: A story seed. A magus's Icelandic apprentice has finished training and accepted a place at a distant spring covenant, which angers a local rival. P. 22.

details.antagonist: A rival who declares Wizard's War on a young covenant

stages.title: The filius's letter
stages.clues: The rival declares Wizard's War on the young magi. The filius writes to his parens that he will not be driven off, and asks for help negotiating a settlement.

stages.title: The Redcap's news
stages.clues: The Redcap bringing the letter also reports that the covenant has been annihilated.
stages.ignored: The filius goes unavenged.

neighbours.name: The Neighbour Whose Harvest Never Fails
neighbours.summary: A story seed. A neighbour of the covenant has good harvests in the worst weather and has grown rich, asking silver, almost unobtainable in Iceland, for his grain and meat. Perhaps a witch charmed his fields with magical stones buried at the boundaries; perhaps he is a friend of the landvaettir. P. 26.

details.antagonist: A greedy neighbour and whoever blesses his land

stages.title: The price in silver
stages.clues: The neighbour prospers and demands silver.

stages.title: The crops fail
stages.clues: His greed has upset his benefactor, whoever that is, and his crops suddenly fail.

neighbours.name: The Lean Year
neighbours.summary: A story seed. Some years even the best farmers cannot feed their households. When it strikes the magi, will they let people starve, and if not, how can they make it up when most of the island is likely as short as they are? P. 26.

neighbours.name: The Sheep in the Canyon
neighbours.summary: A story seed. The covenant's livestock goes missing, always in one canyon deep in the mountains. The shepherds find a giant is taking them, and he seems beyond defeating. Bargaining may be the only way, once someone is found who speaks the giants' language. P. 26.

details.antagonist: A giant ten times the height of a man

neighbours.name: Money for Nothing
neighbours.summary: Storyguide advice from the book, kept as a story. Iceland's economy is tiny beside the mainland's, and Hermetic magic makes precious metal easily. Storyguides should weigh what conjured wealth would do, and may wish to discourage it. P. 25.

details.antagonist: The magi's own conjured silver, and King Hakon

stages.title: Silver loses its value
stages.clues: New silver is noticed almost at once and quickly cheapens in local exchange, leaving it good only for trade with Norwegian merchants.

stages.title: The merchants notice
stages.clues: Merchants soon see how much silver Icelanders hold. More ships come, which helps Iceland.

stages.title: Rumours reach King Hakon
stages.clues: Talk of silver mines sharpens King Hakon's wish for overlordship.

neighbours.name: Between Magic and Faerie
neighbours.summary: A story seed. Merinita magi may be fascinated by landvaettir, which unlike mainland faeries are as at home in magical auras as in faerie ones. What that means could take a lifetime to work out. P. 33.
