neighbours.name: The Logberg (Law Rock)
neighbours.summary: The rock at the Althing where the lawspeaker formally recites new laws. Anyone may stand on the grassy slope around it to offer corrections and argue points of law (LFI p. 36).

neighbours.name: The Law of Iceland
neighbours.summary:
Iceland has no king; it has law. The first settlers, fleeing the feudal order growing on the mainland, framed it around the rights of free men, and the land itself kept any lord from holding wide territories, so wealth lay remarkably evenly. Slaves were freed and freedmen came to own land. That levelling is slowly and painfully coming undone in this century: the law was never able to restrain the storgodar, or later the bishops.

Everyone belongs to the law through a thing attachment. A householder chooses a godi to be in thing with at the spring assembly, and those attached to the household follow that choice, so every person stands with one godi, in one district, in one Quarter (LFI p. 34).

On paper the land looks punished at every turn: eating meat on a Friday can earn lesser outlawry, and tripping a man full outlawry. In truth most offences never reach a court. The one wronged lets the matter go or settles at once, because a suit is costly, slow, technical and often dangerous (LFI pp. 37-38).

The laws are written now, in many books that may differ on the very detail a case turns on, for the law still bears the marks of its oral beginnings. The name Gragas (Grey Goose) belongs to two later manuscripts, and Icelanders of 1220 do not use it (LFI p. 36).

Law reaches everyone. Even magi who shun their neighbours have companions and grogs to feed, and will buy from the farms nearby (LFI p. 39).

details.rules:
Penalties (LFI p. 37): only three exist, each fixed for its crime, and the court cannot vary them. No office enforces them: an unpaid fine needs a new case for non-payment (penalty: lesser outlawry), and after an outlawry the family must post a bounty or hunt the man themselves.

Three-mark fine (24 law ounces): for petty offences such as unintended damage by cattle, small legal errors and minor religious breaches. Half goes to the prosecutor, half to the lawspeaker if present.

Lesser outlawry: three years' banishment, usually for negligent damage above five law ounces and many religious matters, such as a priest forgetting the holy water for a baptism. The outlaw has three summers to find passage; the three years run from then, and he may return with full rights. A court of confiscation divides his property; if it strays from the law the case can be quashed and those responsible face lesser outlawry themselves.

Full outlawry: for any assault that landed a blow, hurt or not, and for breaking judgment in a lesser outlawry case. The outlaw loses all property and all legal, family and Church rights, and the Church always excommunicates him. No one may lawfully help or even advise him, and anyone may kill him. Only surviving twenty years or killing three other outlaws wins a reprieve without the prosecutor's consent.

Court of confiscation: two weeks after the thing that pronounces outlawry, at the convicted man's home, with twelve judges named by a local godi.

Wergild (LFI p. 37): free man 120 law ounces, freedman 60, slave 12; a fraction for harm short of death, not only bodily. It is owed whether or not a suit is brought, unless the victim fell having forfeited immunity. If it goes unpaid, the victim's kin may forbid the attacker's kin from coming near them, who must then humbly keep out of their way.

Principals and vengeance (LFI p. 38): every prosecution and defence needs a principal, who may hand the case to another at any point. A defence principal charged with violence is barred from things and must do so. Assault, injury, raids on property, insult by word or gesture and sexual offences against kinswomen give a right of vengeance: the aggressor loses immunity and may be killed or hurt without penalty, until the next Althing. Forfeit immunity is a common defence.

Advocates (LFI p. 38): any slip, or possible slip, in a major case can spawn a new case. Handing a case to a godi is often very dear, but against a godi the only other course is to drop it. Skill at law can offset uneven support.

Before court (LFI p. 38): the prosecutor publishes the charge before a panel of neighbours, then before them summons the defence principal and tells his witnesses to attend. A killer must publish the deed as his own within a set time and distance, though not before a panel; failing that it is murder, a shameful thing, and full outlawry. Where witnesses are lacking, or intent or state of mind is in question, a panel decides: a panel of neighbours (five or nine freemen, usually those living closest), or a panel of twelve (the local godi and eleven freemen of his assembly third), used for matters of great public interest such as sorcery, theft, murder and perjury.

In court (LFI pp. 38-39): a principal brings at most ten men, and spectators stay beyond the boundary lines. Each litigant draws one lot for the order of cases, however many he has. The prosecutor names his witnesses, swears it is his case, recites his summons and presents his proof. Facts stated within a case may not conflict, and only a perjury judgment of the Fifth Court can amend them, for which the trial may be halted. Witnesses give one testimony, the majority prevailing, and dissenters are immune from perjury. The defence may challenge panel members (someone closer not called, kinship with the prosecutor, means, health), the prosecutor replacing them with the best qualified present; a wrong type of panel, or a witness on the same point, vetoes its verdict, for testimony outranks a panel. The defence then puts its case and the prosecutor may challenge likewise. One judge sums up each side.

Settlement (LFI pp. 39-40): self-judgment, where the victim sets the terms, is the most honourable course, and abusing it costs reputation. Formal duels were outlawed in the eleventh century, though single combat quietly goes on. The summons is the first chance to settle, and refusing a generous offer weakens the prosecutor. Men of rank may call in an arbitrator, or a respected one may step in unasked; only overwhelming support then keeps a case alive. Arbitrators count the dead on each side, offset by rank and other injuries, and make up the difference with compensation on top of wergild. One who cannot pay suffers a banishment whose terms are entirely at the arbitrator's discretion.

neighbours.secrets:
Once the characters are known to exist, even with their covenant unfound, powerful bondi and godi may court them as allies, and others who feel threatened may plot against them. Either way, with Icelandic politics as turbulent as they are, the law will soon be involved (LFI p. 39).

A godi can in practice dictate a panel of twelve, at some cost in respect, and so can shield a magician from an unjust prosecution for sorcery (LFI p. 38).

neighbours.name: The Spring Things
neighbours.summary:
The local assembly (varthing) of each of Iceland's thirteen districts, held by the end of the fourth week of summer, mostly for cases between people of the same district. Every householder (bondi) must attend, in person or by proxy (LFI pp. 34-35).

Each district has three chieftaincies. There were once twelve districts and nine chieftaincies to a Quarter, until the north demanded a fourth district; three more chieftaincies were added to the others to keep the balance, so each Quarter now has twelve. Only the original nine are called full and ancient.

details.rules:
Only godar of full and ancient chieftaincies preside in the eastern, southern and western Quarters (LFI p. 34).

Court of prosecution (LFI pp. 35-36): opens the assembly. 36 judges, twelve named by each godi from his thingmen. A verdict needs 31 to agree; failing that, the case goes to the matching Quarter Court. Godar cannot sit as judges and are free to fight cases and broker settlements.

Court of payments (LFI p. 35): opens four days later. Debts are settled and goods valued, and it sets local measures such as the silver value of the standard ounce and the prices of cloth, fish and livestock.

neighbours.name: The Althing
neighbours.summary:
The General Assembly, held at Thingvoll once ten weeks of summer have passed and lasting at least two weeks. It is the great social event of the year as well as the seat of the law.

The allsherjargodi, the supreme chieftain, opens it. The title goes with the hereditary chieftaincy of Thorstein Ingolfsson, son of Iceland's first settler; for all its grandeur it brings no privilege beyond these duties (LFI p. 35).

details.rules:
All godar and the lawspeaker must be present on the opening day. Each godi should bring at least one in nine of his thingmen, or be fined (LFI p. 35).

The calendar (LFI pp. 35-36): Thursday evening, the allsherjargodi hallows the site and sets the boundaries of the assembly's sections. Friday, judges are appointed. Saturday, either side in a case may challenge or dismiss nominees. Sunday, the bishops lead masses. Monday, the courts convene for nine days, ending on a Wednesday. Last comes the session of the law council, then the weapon-taking.

Weapons may not be carried once the Althing is convened: they stay at the booth or campsite until the weapon-taking, when people pack for home (LFI p. 36).

links.note: Reports the Althing to the districts

neighbours.name: The Quarter Courts
neighbours.summary: The judicial arm of the Althing: one court for each Quarter, hearing what the spring courts could not decide (LFI p. 36).

details.rules: Each holder of a full and ancient godord names one thingman to each court, so each has 36 judges. As in the varthing, a verdict must be all but unanimous: 31 of 36 (LFI pp. 36, 39). A divided judgment goes to the next court up, usually the Fifth Court.

neighbours.name: The Fifth Court
neighbours.summary: The highest court, hearing divided judgments from the Quarter Courts and abuses of procedure itself, such as perjury and bribery (LFI p. 36).

details.rules: All the godar name one judge each, making 48; the accused and the plaintiff each dismiss six for every dispute, leaving 36. A simple majority decides. A tie goes to the prosecution, except in a case sent up from a divided Quarter Court, when lots are drawn. Procedure otherwise follows the lower courts (LFI pp. 36, 39). The book dates its founding to 1004 here and to 1005 in its timeline (LFI p. 17).

neighbours.name: The Law Council (Logretta)
neighbours.summary: The legislative arm of the Althing. Here the chieftains review old laws and make new ones, approve out-of-court settlements, decide disagreements over the law and grant exemptions from it. Its session is the Althing's last official business (LFI pp. 35-36).

details.decides: The 48 godar and two bishops, with the lawspeaker in the chair and holding the casting vote.
details.rules: Every free man may attend, but only godar and bishops may speak; all 48 godar and both bishops must attend. Each godi has two advisers. They sit on three concentric rings of benches, the godar in the middle, the advisers on the inner and outer. The council elects the lawspeaker, and may ask him to recite any part of the law it needs (LFI p. 36).

neighbours.name: The Lawspeaker
neighbours.summary:
The only paid office in Iceland, held for three years by election of the law council. He chairs the council, recites new laws at the Logberg, announces licences for mitigation of penalty and settles the legal calendar for the coming year. Before the laws were written he recited a third of them in each year of his term; now he need recite only those made or repealed that year (LFI pp. 35-36).

In 1220 the office is held by Teit Thorvaldsson the Priest. Snorri Sturluson, back from Norway this year, has let it be known that he will seek re-election in 1222 (LFI p. 36).

details.rules: Stipend of 40 law ounces a year, plus half the fines levied at the Althing and at his own spring assembly. He holds the council's casting vote. Each godi, or two of his advisers, must attend the recital. At a lapse of memory or a hard point he consults at least five legal experts (LFI p. 36).

neighbours.name: The Fall Things
neighbours.summary: The least formal of the three great assemblies, held when eight weeks of summer remain and lasting no more than two days. It tells the people what happened at the Althing: the new laws, official pronouncements such as outlawries, and next year's calendar (LFI pp. 36-37).

details.rules: No court is appointed.

neighbours.name: The Aesir (The Old Religion)
neighbours.summary:
Until the end of the first millennium most Icelanders were pagans, honouring the Norse gods and goddesses together called the Aesir: above all Thor, god of farmers and seafarers, and also Frey, god of fertility. Even the sons of the few Christian settlers took up these ways (LFI p. 41).

Icelanders still recite the myths with pride, take personal belief lightly and are often of two minds about the old faith. Above all, its ideals of honour and vengeance still rule Icelandic life at every level (LFI p. 42).

neighbours.name: The Church in Iceland
neighbours.summary:
Iceland took the faith by a settlement at law. Pressure from the mainland began in 980 and came to a head under King Olaf Tryggvasson (995-1000). His first envoy, the Icelander Stefnir Thorgilsson, wrecked sanctuaries so zealously that he was outlawed and driven off. The priest Thangbrand then won over several prominent men in three years and killed three poets who mocked him, but left in 999 with most Icelanders still pagan. Olaf closed his ports to Icelanders and took the kinsmen of leading pagans hostage in Norway, threatening to maim or kill them.

At the next Althing the parties skirmished and civil war drew near until mediators put the matter to arbitration. Both sides accepted Godi Thorgeir Thorkelsson, a pagan with strong Christian kin. He lay under his cloak for part of a day and a night, and bound both sides to his ruling before giving it: all should be Christian and be baptized, while the exposure of infants and the eating of horseflesh stayed lawful, and private sacrifice was tolerated unless witnessed, when it was lesser outlawry. These allowances were dropped a few years later. So in the summer of 1000 the whole country converted, almost without blood (LFI pp. 41-42).

Iceland then fell under the archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen and was largely neglected. Few foreign priests and wandering missionary bishops came, so farmers built churches at their own expense, and many godar traded their pagan role for the priesthood and served in them. The Church grew into the secular law, its wealth and power run by laymen (LFI p. 42).

The first native bishop, Isleif Gizursson (born about 1006), won little respect, competing with missionary bishops of the Armenian and Eastern Churches. His eldest son Gizur Isleifsson took pledges from all the chieftains to accept his ordinances, was consecrated in 1082, introduced the tithe in 1096 and gave the see a fixed seat by willing it his farm at Skalholt. A second see followed at Holar, and in 1106 the archbishop of Lund consecrated Jon Ogmundarson to it (LFI p. 43).

Reform came late. Thorlak Thorhallsson of Skalholt (1178-93) was the first bishop to try enforcing Church discipline, and in 1190 the archbishop wrote forbidding the ordination of godar. When Thorlak moved against the wardens, Jon Loftsson refused the archbishop's message and rallied them against him (LFI p. 43).

In 1220 priests of every rank still live much as laymen: they marry, keep concubines, inherit, prosecute cases, bear arms and join in feuds and blood vengeance. Orders forbid them weapons and all lawsuits save those of the defenceless, and are ignored. Godar are no longer ordained and few remain priests, but most Church property stays firmly with the lay wardens (LFI p. 43).

details.rules:
Knowing the Pater noster and Credo by heart is required of anyone able to learn them; wilful failure is lesser outlawry, and the bishop decides who prosecutes (LFI p. 42).

The tithe, from 1096, is a 1% property tax split into four: bishop, parish church, priest and paupers (LFI pp. 42-43).

Both bishops sit in the law council (LFI p. 36).

neighbours.name: Skalholt
neighbours.summary: The seat of the southern see, in the south-west, on the farm Bishop Gizur Isleifsson willed to the Church. Eighty people live here around the wooden cathedral (LFI pp. 42-44).

neighbours.name: Holar
neighbours.summary: The seat of the northern see, the second in Iceland, with its cathedral school (LFI pp. 42-43).

neighbours.name: Diocese of Skalholt
neighbours.summary:
A wooden cathedral almost 50 paces long, seat of a diocese of 220 churches and 290 priests. Bishop Magnus Gizurarson lives here in relative quiet (LFI p. 44).

The Southern Bishopric, all the island beyond the Northern Bishopric's bounds (LFI p. 10).

After Bishop Thorlak died in 1193 the chieftains took care to choose men to their liking: Pall Jonsson, and on his death in 1211 Magnus, elected by the godar (LFI p. 43).

neighbours.name: Diocese of Holar
neighbours.summary:
The northern diocese, of 108 parish churches and 136 priests. Its first bishop, Jon Ogmundarson, was consecrated in 1106 (LFI p. 43).

The Northern Bishopric, the middle of the north coast and the land behind it (LFI p. 10).

When the see fell vacant in 1201 the chieftain Kolbeinn Tumason arranged the election of an illegitimate relative of his wife, Gudmund Arason. Gudmund was known for his miracles but thought unfit to run a great institution, and Kolbeinn meant to rule through him. He misjudged: they fell out over alms to the poor and over jurisdiction in cases against clergy, each ignoring the other's rulings, while outlaws took refuge and excommunications went unheeded. Gudmund gathered unruly men and violence followed, until in 1208 a thrown stone killed Kolbeinn.

The chieftains then allied, and from 1209 blocked Gudmund's reforms, often by force. Summoned to Norway by the archbishop in 1214, he found little support there. Since returning in 1218 he has given up the claim to wider judicial power and stands instead as champion of the poor, giving most of the diocese's income to charity when he can (LFI p. 43).

neighbours.name: The Lay Wardens
neighbours.summary:
Godar and well-off farmers who hold Church property. A family grants land in a saint's name and keeps control of it by serving as warden, and donations to the church pass through its hands, so that this control is worth a great deal (LFI p. 42).

Led by Jon Loftsson, they turned back Bishop Thorlak's attempt to take control from them, armed though he was with the archbishop's letter (LFI p. 43).

details.rules: A warden receives two of the tithe's four parts, the church's and the priest's, keeps any profit, and is personally exempt from the tithe (LFI p. 43).

neighbours.name: Reykjadal
neighbours.summary: The region of the northern diocese where Bishop Gudmund's company now wanders, and where its farmers are running out of patience (LFI pp. 43-44).

neighbours.name: Bishop Gudmund's Following
neighbours.summary: Bishop Gudmund Arason lives in poverty among clergy, armed men, vagrants, beggars and thieves. He keeps 120 followers moving about Reykjadal, demanding hospitality from the local farmers (LFI pp. 43-44).

neighbours.name: The School at Oddi
neighbours.summary: Founded by Saemundur Sigfusson (1056-1133), who was sent abroad as a youth to further his training as a priest, learned Natural Magic in France, and came home to be consulted on many matters. His son Eyjolf became its headmaster. Saemundur joined the learned art to the song magic of the Icelandic galdor: where natural magicians usually work their will directly, his spells conjured an airy spirit to do the deed. Many Icelandic magicians took up this theurgy, though its roots are heathen (LFI p. 42).

neighbours.name: Skalholt Cathedral School
neighbours.summary: One of the two cathedral schools, each with its centre for the study of magic. Its magicians are priests, often indiscreet, whose office puts them beyond reproach; they are credited with prophecy through astronomy. Fewer than two dozen schooled galdramen exist at any one time, between the schools. Skalholt's name is unstained: its members use their art only for the good of their flock (LFI p. 42).
neighbours.secrets: It seeks a breakthrough to match the feats of Iceland's pagan magicians, as Holar does (LFI p. 42).

neighbours.name: Holar Cathedral School
neighbours.summary: The northern of the two cathedral schools, each with its centre for the study of magic. Its magicians are priests, often indiscreet, whose office puts them beyond reproach; they are credited with prophecy through astronomy (LFI p. 42).
neighbours.secrets: The two schools have drifted apart, and Holar has grown darker: it is whispered that it uses magic to enslave true demons. It too seeks a breakthrough to match the feats of Iceland's pagan magicians (LFI p. 42).

neighbours.name: Thingeyrar
neighbours.summary: Home of a small Benedictine monastery (LFI p. 44).

neighbours.name: Thingeyrar Monastery
neighbours.summary:
A Benedictine house founded in 1112, a centre of learning and instruction. Icelandic monasteries seldom hold more than ten monks, and are often set up with the help of a godi or bondi who then retires to them.

Like all Iceland's houses it is tiny, poor and hard put to make ends meet, with scribes who both copy and write (LFI p. 44).

neighbours.name: Munkathvera
neighbours.summary: Home of a small Benedictine monastery (LFI p. 44).

neighbours.name: Munkathvera Monastery
neighbours.summary:
A Benedictine house founded in 1155, a centre of learning and instruction. Icelandic monasteries seldom hold more than ten monks, and are often set up with the help of a godi or bondi who then retires to them.

Like all Iceland's houses it is tiny, poor and hard put to make ends meet, with scribes who both copy and write (LFI p. 44).

neighbours.name: Thykkvibaer
neighbours.summary: Home of a small Augustinian monastery (LFI p. 44).

neighbours.name: Thykkvibaer Monastery
neighbours.summary:
A Augustinian house founded in 1168, a centre of learning and instruction. Icelandic monasteries seldom hold more than ten monks, and are often set up with the help of a godi or bondi who then retires to them.

Like all Iceland's houses it is tiny, poor and hard put to make ends meet, with scribes who both copy and write (LFI p. 44).

neighbours.name: Kirkjubaer
neighbours.summary: Home of a small Benedictine monastery (LFI p. 44).

neighbours.name: Kirkjubaer Monastery
neighbours.summary:
A Benedictine house founded in 1186, a centre of learning and instruction. Icelandic monasteries seldom hold more than ten monks, and are often set up with the help of a godi or bondi who then retires to them.

Like all Iceland's houses it is tiny, poor and hard put to make ends meet, with scribes who both copy and write (LFI p. 44).

neighbours.name: Videy
neighbours.summary: The site of a planned Augustinian monastery, not yet built (LFI p. 44).
neighbours.secrets: The map (p. 10) marks it as a monastery already.

neighbours.name: Helgafell
neighbours.summary: On the Snaefellsnes peninsula, with a small monastery.

neighbours.name: Helgafell Monastery
neighbours.summary: A small house on the Snaefellsnes peninsula.
neighbours.secrets: Printed only on the map (p. 10). The list of houses on p. 44 leaves it out, and no order or date is given.

neighbours.name: Kirkjubaer Nunnery
neighbours.summary: The nunnery at Kirkjubaer, founded in 1186 and home to seven nuns under an Abbess. It is nearly self-sufficient, yet in financial trouble and under the control of Skalholt (LFI p. 44).

neighbours.name: The Outlaw's Son
neighbours.summary: A man the covenant cannot do without proves to be the son of an outlaw, a vargdropi ('wolf-droppings'), which by law leaves him as exposed as his father. The father killed a man and his kin paid no blood money, so the dead man's sons want his blood too (LFI p. 39).

details.antagonist: The sons of the murdered man

neighbours.secrets: The safest road is to have a court rule on his status and, with luck, declare him free. That takes careful politics, for he has enemies well placed.

neighbours.name: Outlawing a Powerful Enemy
neighbours.summary: An outlaw may be killed by anyone, so the surest answer to a mighty foe is to have him outlawed. But a powerful man has powerful friends even when the facts are against him, and in Iceland power means a deep hand in politics (LFI p. 39).

neighbours.name: A Covenant Needs Land
neighbours.summary: A covenant is a household, and in Iceland no household can appear from nowhere and claim land. All usable farmland has an owner whose family lives by it and will not gladly sell. Tenancy is demeaning and open to the landlord's demands; being a bondi is hard to reach, best done by inheriting, and brings many obligations (LFI p. 39).

neighbours.name: The Nuns of Kirkjubaer
neighbours.summary: The nuns must find enough to live on or Skalholt will disband them, and word of rich foreign scholars has reached them (LFI p. 44).

stages.title: The Abbess petitions the covenant
stages.clues: She journeys to the magi herself to ask for aid.
stages.ignored: Skalholt disbands the nuns.
stages.stopped: A gift is easily borne by the covenant, wins much good will and eases fear of the foreign magicians.

stages.title: The monasteries come asking
stages.clues: Only if the covenant was too generous to the nuns.

neighbours.name: Galdramen Hreppur
neighbours.summary:
Iceland's magicians long ago did what its farmers do, and made a hreppur of their own: a cooperative that sets their fees, shares out common land and common duties, and settles the quarrels no thing could be asked to hear. It meets once a year at Eldborg in the Western Quarter, five days after the Althing ends, and it has a bargain with the godar: the paths across the interior are kept warded against trolls and violent spirits, and its people are not hounded.

It began in the tenth century, when godar were pressing magicians to meddle in feuds. A magician who felt that pressure had the whole hreppur behind him, and the godar soon thought better of it. Charms and spells that meant no harm were sold at fixed prices to all but the blacklisted, and the hreppur came to regulate the gathering of ond, the vital force that Odin gave to man in the old tale and Latin magi call vis, which galdramen give to the spirits. Its people have also treated with giants and dragons to keep the peace. Volur and visindamen were first asked to join in the Interdiction of 1031-1041 (pp. 11-12, 14, 17, 27-29).

details.decides: A council, sitting yearly at Eldborg; it also judges disputes between members (p. 28)
details.rules:
Fees (1220): a trollson, galdraman or vitkir charges one standard ounce a day or part of a day, to two standard marks (16 ounces) a season. Seithkona and witches charge half an ounce a day, to one mark (8 ounces) a season. Ond is charged at one standard mark a pawn.
Discretion: magic is to be discreet, with as few witnesses as may be. A householder hiring a magician first assures him none of the household will take offence; if that fails, the magician is not answerable. Supernatural affairs are not discussed with non-members unless it cannot be helped, and the council alone decides what men of rank must be told. A member charged with witchcraft through unjustified, indiscreet magic pays the godi or storbaendur who defends him six law marks; if it was beyond his control the defence is free.
Ond: a member may claim any source on his own land; on common land the first to harvest it claims it. A poacher returns the ond and pays a mark a pawn. The claims of a member dying without an heir lie open to the first harvester; abandoned sites may be claimed, and the hreppur judges any dispute.
Duties: the cost and work of the path wards is split as evenly as the members allow. One who cannot contribute gives at least three pawns a year; one too poor for that pays nothing, but may not judge or sit on the council. Serving anyone on the blacklist, reviewed yearly, costs a fine of three law marks and the fee taken.
Black magic: malign magic on a human forfeits the hreppur's protection; magical attacks are allowed only against outlawed magicians. A magician in a mundane conflict uses mundane means or loses that protection. Attacked at home or on an innocent journey, not on a raid, he may use magic to drive off attackers or get away, but only with his life at risk, and never to injure on purpose.
details.wants: Its members left in peace by the godar, its magic discreet, its trade orderly, and no talk of it among outsiders
details.offers: Fixed fees for magical service; wards on the interior paths; a court for what cannot go to the things; a godi's defence against a charge of witchcraft

neighbours.secrets:
Its authority is loose: no oath, no ceremony of joining, and attending Eldborg or paying the path tax is voluntary, but only those who keep its laws share the protection of its deal with the godar. Magi may be admitted on the same terms. Witchcraft cases embarrass it badly, and it works to end them fast (pp. 102, 105).

The meeting in the book's saga draws 11 trollsynir, 6 vitkir, 62 galdramen (11 of them schooled) and 8 seithkonur, with a council of five (p. 102).

With the Guardians at its side it could stand even against Hermetic magi. Kill a prominent galdraman and many landvaettir lords are incensed; kill a trollson and his giant kin are enraged; a war could turn all of supernatural Iceland on the Order (p. 29).

neighbours.name: Icelandic Magicians
neighbours.summary: The island has its own ways of magic, far from the roots of Hermes: song that calls the land's spirits, giants' blood, runes cut and reddened, shapes taken and shapes forced on others, curses set on a horse-headed pole in sight of an enemy's farm. Latin magi call their makers hedge wizards. An Icelander who sees a nidstong knocks it down on the spot.

details.rules:
The rules are on the sheet of anyone who belongs to the tradition; Help has How to play a galdraman.
Limits (p. 45): those peculiar to Norse magic are for Norse characters, at the storyguide's careful choice. Hermetic Virtues are open to the Gifted (Hedge Magic RE p. 12); trollsynir have no other shapeshifting power and nothing of a realm at odds with theirs.
Virtues: Mighty Fylgja and Large Fylgja, Hamfarir, Potency, Curse, Jotunn Affinity with Earth, Galdor Conjuring, Galdor Enchantment. The book's other Talents are the gruagach Arts, or Rival Magic's Winter's Breath, Storm's Eye, Wildfire and Sjonhverfing. The book's Gift has no Ability: keep its score in notes (pp. 57-58).
Nidstong (pp. 57-59): a tall rune-cut pole topped with a horse's skull, set overlooking the victims' land; it can strike groups. A casting roll daily against each target until it succeeds, with no backlash or botch while it stands; the last rolls count when it falls.
Lifting a Curse (p. 59): the maker beats the first roll; or the condition is met. A Curse holder beating the total, or an Intellego Vim of the 7th magnitude, learns the condition. Intellego Vim of 20+ shows the Ease Factor, and a Perdo Vim ritual above the casting total dispels it, at the risk of catching it on a botch.
Sun Duration (p. 51): in Iceland D: Sun lasts to the next sunrise or sunset, from about 23 hours at midsummer to 1, and further north longer. Optionally a full turn of the sky breaks it, at just under 24 hours.

neighbours.name: Traditional Galdramen
neighbours.summary:
Norse theurgists whose art is galdor, song-magic: long chants of sacred phrases, heavy with the old Aesir stories, that call the spirits of the land to serve. A galdraman spends his life learning the landvaettir of his country and composing poems in their honour, and he will sing from a wooden platform or a chair, since the magic turns sullen against the bare ground. When he stops singing, it stops. He knows his own land's spirits only, and in a strange country must begin again.

They are mostly men; a woman of the tradition is a galdrakona, and few there are. The Gift marks them, with all its unease. Though they may be pagans at heart, they need no temple for their magic, and so have escaped the Church's wrath.

A galdraman's fylgja leads his spirit into Twilight, and at the last does not bring it home.

details.rules:
The rules are on the sheet of anyone who belongs to the tradition; Help has How to play a galdraman.
The tradition's chapter is Galdor; its More has Conjure a Spirit, Bargain with a Lord and Bind an Item (pp. 45-50, 54).
Health (pp. 48-49): no Instant effects. Lim- and biarg-galdor spirits add the magnitude to recovery rolls, attending at least 12 hours in 24; a ritual conjuring with vis can rival Hermetic cures.
Longevity (pp. 49-50): with biarg-galdor, a lord grants it for a service besides vis, by anyone's hand. He then drinks mead with a pawn per decade of age and conjures a biarg spirit by ritual: a longevity potion of the conjuring total. Yearly mead renews it; it never fails, even on an aging result. Typical services: pull down a Christian shrine on magical ground, free a captive spirit, drive out a diabolist who tortures spirits, make a charm to clean a stream.
Hermetic Potential (p. 51): one who joins the Order learns Parma Magica but no Arts. Optionally, with the Mysteries, a crippled theurgic magic may be shared with a Hermetic theurgist.
details.wants: Good standing with the landvaettir lords, whose servants do their work, and their old lore left unmolested
details.offers: Spirits called by song for healing, weather, sight of far places, wards on a path or a farm, and curses

links.note: Sits in the hreppur at Eldborg

neighbours.name: Schooled Galdramen
neighbours.summary:
Priests trained at the cathedral schools of Holar and Skalholt, who weave divine names with animals, plants, stones, images, aromatics, talismans and written letters into intricate rites, to call the spirits as the old galdramen do. The way was opened by Saemundur Sigfusson, who came home from France and put Judeo-Christian and classical phrases in place of the heathen ones. All are clergy, so none are women.

Mainland scholars would call the method dangerous and the theory heresy, but Iceland is far off and a law unto itself, and no churchman of rank who has learned of it has yet made an issue of it.

details.rules:
Learned Magicians (Hedge Magic RE, Chapter 5), Iceland's Natural Magicians (pp. 45, 51), whose sacred phrases are synthemata.
They conjure magical spirits to make the effect. The only differences: they use the normal magical interaction table, and they have the Gift.
details.offers: The same services, worked with Christian learning

links.note: Sits in the hreppur at Eldborg
The Virtues and limits they share

neighbours.secrets: Being Gifted, they could learn Hermetic magic; they only lack the means. Books of Hermetic theory in either school could change that, to the horror of the Order (p. 51).

neighbours.name: Trollsynir
neighbours.summary:
The sons of trolls (a man is a trollson, a woman a trollsdottir): wizards whose power is their giant blood, seldom more than three generations from a giant forebear. Each belongs to a giant clan whose ways shape him. Raised by giants or by grown trollsynir, they soak up magic as other children do speech, and know little of men. Most share their elders' hostility to mankind; a rare few turn their gifts to good. They speak Jotunn, and they are the Norse cousins of Scotland's gruagachan, though not the same.

Their magic costs them. Each slip brings them nearer the wild blood, with horns or fangs or blue skin, until the mind goes too and they flee to the wilderness. Many of Iceland's trolls are said to have been trollsynir. Some choose to break their own soulstones first.

details.decides: No one: they have no formal organisation (p. 54)
details.rules:
The rules are on the sheet of anyone who belongs to the tradition; Help has How to play a galdraman.
The Fifth Edition trollsynir of Hedge Magic RE p. 76: the gruagach Arts through the Jotnar tongue, with a Trollskap chapter. No Magic Resistance (Hedge Magic RE p. 9) and no Potency, so totals fall from the book's; Afflictions are Transformation's bad results. A printed figure stays in a record's notes.
details.wants: Mostly to be left alone, away from men
details.offers: Rarely, and from a very few, their powers to men's benefit

links.note: Sits in the hreppur at Eldborg
The Virtues and limits they share

neighbours.name: Vitkir of Iceland
neighbours.summary: Rune-magicians who draw on the pagan Norse gods. They are rare here, for the law comes down hard on heathen ways, and a vitki in Iceland all but needs a magic or faerie regio to hide his patron's temple in. In the old days godar who wanted power mostly gave up their arts to keep it. Vitkir sit in the Galdramen Hreppur, charge its higher fee, and can ward the interior paths as galdramen do.

details.rules: The tradition is Ultima Thule's. Pp. 9, 12, 28, 45.

links.note: Sits in the hreppur at Eldborg

neighbours.name: Volur
neighbours.summary: The name Icelanders often give a woman who practises magic (a volva, in the singular): the witches and seeresses who came with the Norse settlers and often worked seithr, a magic of shamanic rites. A few are galdrakona, among the traditional galdramen; others are seithkonur. No woman is a schooled galdraman, for those are all clergy.

neighbours.name: Visindamen
neighbours.summary: The wise men among the Norse magicians who came with the settlers, often workers of seithr as the volur are. They stood outside the hreppur until the Interdiction.

details.rules: The book gives them no rules of their own. Pp. 9, 14.

neighbours.name: Seithkonur
neighbours.summary: Women magicians, among the volur, each of whom can borrow her fylgja's body and go abroad in it. The hreppur allows them only half the fee of a galdraman, half an ounce a day.

details.rules: Folk Witches (Hedge Magic RE, Chapter 3), each with a fylgja and Hamfarir, Second Sight and Legend Lore instead of Visions and the faerie versions. Pp. 28, 45, 55, 65.

links.note: Sits in the hreppur at Eldborg

neighbours.name: The Order of Odin
neighbours.summary: The band of Norse wizards that senior magi of the Order of Hermes fear, on very little evidence, and fear the more for having so little.

links.note: What the Order would mistake for it

neighbours.secrets:
Whether it exists is for each storyguide to decide. On the surface the Galdramen Hreppur looks like this Order, but it grew up here, shaped by local custom and local wants, and owes nothing to anyone abroad. Icelanders mentioned the name will only be confused (pp. 29, 105). That hedge wizards can resist Hermetics at all would still confirm the Order's fears.

The Icelandic Wars keeps it a phantom: a century of rumour and destroyed spring covenants in Norse lands drive the Order's fear, searches find only weak hedge wizards who have never heard the name, and neither Pan Caudarax nor any Icelandic magician knows of it. Who destroyed those covenants the book never says (Icelandic Wars pp. 1-3, 12).

neighbours.name: The Order against the Hreppur
neighbours.summary:
Fearful magi take Iceland's magicians for the Order of Odin and move against them, and the deaths draw landvaettir lords, giant kin and the Guardians into the quarrel. The characters may stand on either side.

Notes: p. 29.

details.antagonist: Hermetic magi who take the hreppur for the Order of Odin

neighbours.name: A Friend's Longevity Bargain
neighbours.summary:
A galdraman the characters respect asks them to settle some matter touching the landvaettir, and does not say it is the service his longevity deal demands. A rival magician works against them, and without knowing it they decide whether the old man sees out the winter.

Notes: p. 49.

details.antagonist: A rival magician, and the winter

neighbours.name: The Lord's Quest
neighbours.summary:
A galdraman seeking a new power is set quests by a lord of the landvaettir, and must earn the story experience to pay for it. The book's examples: make peace between the men of Vapnafjord and the trolls of the Eastern Quarter; bring the magic spear of the rune-magician Viga-Glum out of the middle of the Odadahraun; find the soul-stone of the giantess Mjoll, so she may die in peace; or persuade the men of Kirkadale to leave their farms for the lowlands.

Notes: p. 50.

details.antagonist: A landvaettir lord who sets the price of teaching

neighbours.name: Hermetic Theory at the Schools
neighbours.summary:
Books on Hermetic theory reach Holar or Skalholt, whose Gifted priests lack only that to learn the Order's magic. A merchant bound for Skalholt is blown off course to Snaefellsnes with Hermetic books for the bishop's school among his cargo, and the magi there must choose what to do. Trade with the schools and monasteries may equally build a library, for books on Philosophiae hold something each side could learn from.

Notes: pp. 27, 51.

details.antagonist: The schooled galdramen of Holar and Skalholt

neighbours.name: The Walrus Hunt
neighbours.summary:
Walrus crowd the western and northern coasts in winter, on the ice floes. They are dangerous to hunt, and rich: ivory, hide, blubber and meat. Not every walrus is a walrus.

Notes: p. 27.

neighbours.name: The Wormhout Regio
neighbours.summary: A stretch of forest a mile outside the town of Wormhout, reached by a clear path that passes between two worn stone pillars.

levels.name: The Manor Level
levels.notes:
Secrets
A manor house among grogs' quarters, stables, a smithy and a meeting hall, entered between the two stone pillars in the forest. Hermetic visitors are lodged in the manor house. Steps at the far end of its main hall rise to a mosaic floor (p. 79).

levels.name: The Tower Level
levels.notes:
Secrets
A huge tower of sanctums, library and council chamber, entered between two carved pillars on the mosaic in the manor hall; only the covenant's magi and consortes may pass (p. 79).

neighbours.secrets:
A two-tier magical regio, with the mundane level guarded by a powerful Mentem spell (pp. 77, 79). Markus's parens designed its gates and seals, the covenant's main defence (p. 78).

The town lies about 42 miles east of Calais and 16 miles southwest of De Panne (p. 77).

neighbours.name: Town of Wormhout
neighbours.summary: A town beside a forest, which has grown greatly in trade and people over the last three centuries.
neighbours.secrets: The covenant of Wormhout lies in the forest just outside (p. 77).

neighbours.name: De Panne
neighbours.summary: A large Flemish port town of about five thousand souls, half a mile from its beach and docks, smelling of soot and fish. Fishing huts line the shore and old docks run far out over the shallows.
neighbours.secrets:
The book's suggested mainland base for Spider in the Ice; it may be moved anywhere in Mythic Europe, and a second storyguide could run stories here (p. 70). Earthen banks replace the land near the waterfront (p. 80).

Pan Caudarax keeps a hoard here, and has promised to raze the town only if that hoard is robbed (p. 63). Once the saga is under way Redcaps deliver and collect at Iain's house and may not tell other magi where it is (p. 75). The local Redcap trades vis on the magi's behalf: a year for each exchange, at most 9 pawns at a time, and a pawn charged for every three.

neighbours.name: The Red Lion
neighbours.summary: A cheerful inn of three joined buildings in De Panne, kept by a grey-bearded man named Pol and his wife Richilda. Rooms are affordable.
neighbours.secrets: Redcaps often stay here and the keeper is especially friendly with the Order. Asked politely, Pol and Richilda say they heard the Englishmen talk of going back to Exeter (pp. 80-81).

neighbours.name: Iain Scot's House
neighbours.summary: A merchant's townhouse facing the square of De Panne, its back to the docks.
neighbours.secrets: Headquarters of Iain's large trading company, whose ship waits in port. Burned in Lord Peter's raid; as the magi arrive the smoke is still rising, and Donncadh blames threats from overseas debtors (p. 80).

neighbours.name: Exeter
neighbours.summary: A busy trading port on the river Exe, two days' sail from De Panne, with a quay for seagoing ships.
neighbours.secrets: The ship that fled De Panne lies here, and its captain fears Lord Peter. Quiet approaches and money get answers; public quarrels get only angry words. The crew were hired for a raid, and were shocked at its being in the middle of the town, and at the fire. Commoners and merchants here think little of Lord Peter (p. 81).

neighbours.name: Coombe
neighbours.summary: A village at the edge of Dartmoor, in hilly country.
neighbours.secrets: Its people avoid the manor nearby, and the servants' families have heard nothing of them for months (p. 81).

neighbours.name: Lord Peter's Manor
neighbours.summary: A manor house on the edge of Dartmoor near Coombe, cut off by the hills.
neighbours.secrets:
Lightly guarded: six men remain when the magi come, in and around the house, and the servants are locked in their sleeping chambers. Set free they are grateful, and wish only to run home to their villages (pp. 81-82).

Lord Peter's private chambers hold what serves a diabolist as a laboratory. In the middle is a stone archway capped with the stolen gatestone, which opens to Scartaris when the keystone is touched and a phrase spoken, and stays open under concentration. Ugly rumours tie him to disappearances among moorland farmers.

neighbours.name: Carnac
neighbours.summary: The great megaliths of Carnac, in France.
neighbours.secrets: One of the lost gateways of the Cult of Thoth stands here, leading to the Kerlingarfjoll valley. Hetep led Damhan-Allaidh through it, he used it again to escape to Scotland after 808, and Victor found it in 845 and took its gatestone to Vindolanda (pp. 71-72). One of Lord Peter's ancestors served Damhan-Allaidh here (p. 83).

neighbours.name: Sir Ivain of De Panne
neighbours.summary: A landed knight in Flanders, loyal to the French Crown, who carries a holy sword.
neighbours.secrets: The hero of the seed The Dragon's Bane (p. 63).

neighbours.name: The Praeses Septentrionalis
neighbours.summary: The Northern Guard, an old league of Hermetic covenants.
neighbours.secrets: Vindolanda joined it to guard Scotland against Damhan-Allaidh's return (p. 72). His forces attacked its covenants in 889 and destroyed them all (pp. 72, 77).

neighbours.name: The Thothian Watchers
neighbours.summary: Spirits of old Egypt, about whom almost nothing is told.
neighbours.secrets: Thoth set them to capture and imprison Hetep, but they cannot take him while he possesses someone. He used to lose them by going back to Hell, which he now cannot do without undoing his partial corruption of the stelae. They speak to no one and wait for his mistake. The book prints no stats. Ealasaid's grimoire holds a spell to contact them, now of little use (p. 84).

neighbours.name: The Odd-Karnor Clan
neighbours.summary: A Norwegian family, embroiled in a feud of its own.
neighbours.secrets: Bjarke Odd-Karnor called in his distant kinsman Einar Gamlisson for magical help in 1210. Einar stayed seven years and married Yrsa, a young girl of the clan (p. 69). She and her two sons died in 1218. The feud is a centuries-old one with the Beogarts, a powerful family in Iceland (p. 103; see Leif Beogart).

neighbours.name: The Ranks of Iceland
neighbours.summary: Who stands where in Iceland: free men, householders, landowners, great farmers and chieftains, and those with no standing.
neighbours.secrets:
The ranks are Social Status Virtues and Flaws now: Bondi, Landowner, Storbondi, Godi and Storgodi; a freeman is a Laborer, a freedman a Freed Slave, and Slave and Outlaw are as they are elsewhere (pp. 65-66). A godi has no serfs or men-at-arms, so he is no Landed Noble.

Every Icelander starts with Icelandic Law 2 and Legend Lore 2. The wealthy, from landowner up, are usually Educated, which they pay for (p. 66).

Iceland-born characters (pp. 64-65). Magus-equivalents: Trollson, traditional galdraman. Mythic companions: seithkona (a Hedge Magic cunning-woman with a fylgja and Hamfarir instead of Visions, and Second Sight and Legend Lore instead of the faerie versions), schooled galdraman (Natural Magician), spirit master. Companions: witch, seeress or wiseman, viking (anachronistic by 1220), skald, shapeshifter, bondi, godi. Grogs: berserker (almost unknown by now), laborer, tenant farmer, thrall.

The book's Fourth Edition Virtue lists (p. 65). Witch (heid), often with a Jotunn Affinity, some with Scribe Runes, Shapeshift or Transform: Bane Maker +2, Magical Animal Companion +2, Herbalism +1, Bad Reputation (pagan) -1, Tainted with Evil -2. Seeress (volva) or wiseman (visindaman): Divination +4, Visions +2, Second Sight +1, Premonitions +1. Viking: Mercenary Leader +3 or Wealthy Merchant +3, Ways of the Sea +4, Well Traveled +1, Social Contacts +1, Berserk +1, Fury -3, Judged Unfairly -1. Skald: Audio Eidetic Memory +3, Free Expression +1, Inspirational +1. Shapeshifter: Shapeshifter +5, Skinchanger +2 or Lycanthrope -3, Outcast -1. Bondi: Bondi +1, Landowner +2, Storbondi +3, Social Contacts +1, Obligations -1. Godi: Godi +4, Prestigious Family +1, Feud -1 to -4. Berserker: Berserk +1, Fury -3, Outcast -1. Laborer: Freeman or Freedman. Tenant farmer: Bondi. Thrall: Slave.

Magi should come from the Order's heartlands, at first; at most one player should fill the magus slot with a native magician. One character needs Premonitions for Spider in the Ice.

neighbours.name: Fire and Song
neighbours.summary:
Driven by a galdraman's grief. Einar Gamlisson has sworn to destroy the family of the dragon that killed his own, and the characters are caught between them.

The book offers this as one saga, not as official Mythic history (p. 67).

details.antagonist: Einar Gamlisson, galdraman, against Pan Caudarax

stages.title: Thord's Feast
stages.clues: A local storbaendur accuses the characters of sorcery, and they go to the district's spring thing. He suffers the side effects of a curse laid on Pan Caudarax's eggs; one young dragon is already dead.
stages.stopped: Lifting the curse wins them a place in Iceland, and tells them someone holds a deep grudge against a dragon.

stages.title: Meet the Dragon
stages.clues: An invitation to the magicians' meeting at Eldborg. The dragon demands to talk to the priests of Hermes, and threatens to lay Iceland waste.
stages.stopped: Appeasing Pan Caudarax also wins the right to gather vis at certain sites.

stages.title: Feast of Thanks
stages.clues: Bard Snaefellsass invites them to a feast of thanks for dealing with the dragon. They learn of Iceland's supernatural powers and are drawn into their quarrels, above all with a clan of giants.
stages.stopped: Some allies won, some enemies defused.

stages.title: The Glittering Plains
stages.clues: 1230 to 1231. The eggs are near hatching and Einar tries again to destroy them, then escapes to the Glittering Plains, a strange realm underground, where the characters follow him and meet its people.
stages.stopped: They may end the feud by diplomacy or violence, and may find the Obsidian Temple.

neighbours.secrets:
The first arc, before the climax with Damhan-Allaidh; its purpose is to draw the characters into Iceland's daily life, where magicians live beside farmers and godar, a small picture of what the Order might achieve in Europe (pp. 67-68). Chapters 11 to 14. Each story follows on the next by the years shown, but the dates are suggestions, not to be enforced, and other stories fill the time between (p. 75).

In 1210 Einar went to Norway to help Bjarke Odd-Karnor, and stayed seven years; he married Yrsa and had two sons. He sailed home a year ahead of them to repair his farmstead and renew his ties with the spirits. In 1218 Yrsa and the boys took ship at Bergen. Powerful Flambeau magi were aboard, going to destroy the Order of Odin. Their presence roused the landvaettir and the First Guardian, Pan Caudarax, who burned the ship and went home to Hekla. Einar does not see that the dragon was defending Iceland (pp. 69-70).

Einar is cunning and ruthless, and the characters may pity him. Pan Caudarax is a huge dragon of the Hekla crater, not native to the north, in Iceland over a thousand years. Bard Snaefellsass, a powerful trollson, wants the two reconciled and holds himself guardian of the land the covenant stands on, so he may become a strong ally (p. 70).

Vis: Vindolanda soon has Rego and Vim sources; beyond that only stories (the Odadahraun among them) and aura extraction bring it. The annual Galdramen Hreppur meeting will haggle for vis, in rough terms such as fire, illusion, warding, weather (p. 75).

The book's dates disagree. The eggs hatch about twenty years after the settlement of 1222 (pp. 105-106), yet are two years from hatching in 1230 (pp. 76, 114). Page 106 puts the burned ship five years back, about 1217, where p. 70 says 1218.

neighbours.name: Spider in the Ice
neighbours.summary:
Driven by the Order's oldest feud. Damhan-Allaidh, the Spider, and the demon Hetep plot from Iceland to bring the Order down, and a hidden valley temple of Thoth is the prize.

The book offers this as one saga, not as official Mythic history (p. 67).

stages.title: Blood of Innocence
stages.clues: The characters are sent to help Iain Scot, an old ally of their covenant. His family guards the gatestone to Victor's sanctum; a diabolist takes it, kidnaps Brighde and forces her to open the gate, and the characters follow him to Iceland and find Victor and Hetep locked in battle. Played out in the story of the same name.
stages.stopped: The diabolist dies, Brighde is possessed by Hetep, then by Victor to bind the demon, and the characters are invited into Vindolanda and make Iceland their base.

stages.title: Brighde's Gauntlet
stages.clues: Her gauntlet is to trick Hetep into showing where Damhan-Allaidh's body lies. He makes for Old Vindolanda and opens a hidden gatestone to Ealasaid's secret sanctum.
stages.ignored: As planned, Hetep tricks Brighde and gets away in Damhan-Allaidh's body, and Victor must sacrifice himself to save her.

stages.title: Spider Through Mist
stages.clues: Hetep and Damhan-Allaidh break into the Kerlingarfjoll valley and the Obsidian Temple.
stages.ignored: Hetep corrupts the stelae and begins to corrupt all magical writing in the world, with Damhan-Allaidh guarding the temple.
stages.stopped: Hetep is thwarted and the magi win.

stages.title: Into the Gateway
stages.clues: The magi finish Ealasaid's work on the Obsidian Gateway ritual. As things stand, they must help defend the stelae or break in to destroy them.
stages.stopped: A last battle with Damhan-Allaidh, Hetep or both ends the arc.

neighbours.secrets:
The second arc: Chapter 9 brings the characters to Iceland and Chapters 15 to 17 end it, about forty years on (pp. 67-68). The fate of Damhan-Allaidh, the valley temple and Vindolanda are at the storyguide's discretion. Its two seats are Iceland and De Panne, which suits a second storyguide (p. 70). Dates are suggestions (p. 75).

The valley. About 2000 BC priests of Thoth under the legendary Setna followed spirits to a mist-shrouded valley at Iceland's heart, and after years broke the mist with a spell. An obsidian block carved into an arch stood there. They built a temple round it and opened a gateway; few who entered came back, but those who did had multiplied power. They made lesser gateways, and when Egypt fell the priests were scattered and the ways lost (pp. 70-71).

The Spider. A Pictish magician drawn to goetia, he got a reed scroll naming Hetep in 680 and made a cardinal pact: ancient knowledge and the safest hiding place for his soul. Hetep took him by Carnac to the valley and hid inside him. Setna's spirit, for once deceived, let him study the seven stelae for four seasons while Hetep corrupted them; then Setna saw it, fought him, and he fled through the seven doors into the Glasvellir regio. He came out of the Snaefell crater in 730. The gate no longer answers him; Hetep says to wait for Setna to weaken (p. 71).

The wars. He refused the Order's offer, and his blood sacrifice and demon cults brought Flambeau and Tremere against him. He beat them in 808, then left by Carnac for Scotland. Pralix of Tytalus landed in Northumbria in May 814 and in two years beat him with local wizards; he escaped. She raised the Ordo Miscellanea from her army, and Trianoma brought it in as House Ex Miscellanea (p. 71). The years are Heirs to Merlin's: founded 815, accepted 817 (p. 13).

Vindolanda. Victor, Pralix's apprentice, whose gauntlet was surviving the war, founded it on a supply fort of Hadrian's Wall with theurgists Ealasaid and Macomb and gruagachan Iain and Liam. In 845 he found the Carnac gate and brought its stone home; seven years on it was deciphered and the valley found. Ealasaid made Hermetic gatestones in three more years, and each magus built a linked sanctum: Victor's in the Scartaris peak of Snaefell, the others beneath the sea off Devon and in Snowdonia (p. 72).

The battle of wills. They captured Hetep in 875 and found him a fallen spirit of Thoth. Victor designed a spell of wills to turn him, which ends only with one's defeat, and the theurgists warded him in with him. It began in 888, and Iain's party left with the Scartaris gatestone. In 889 the Spider destroyed the Northern Guard and led the attack on Vindolanda; Ealasaid and Macomb died. Liam escaped. In 890 Tremere and Flambeau routed the Spider's forces, and he and Liam were buried in Ealasaid's collapsing sanctum under 50 meters of sea, their external souls keeping them alive. His last followers fled to Shetland and some to Iceland, and Hetep's minions still hunt the sanctum (pp. 71-73).

neighbours.name: Blood of Innocence
neighbours.summary:
Driven by a diabolist's bargain. A wounded merchant is carried into Wormhout, his house burned and his granddaughter stolen, and the treaty he invokes sends the covenant's young guests after her.

The book offers this as one saga, not as official Mythic history (p. 67).

details.antagonist: Lord Peter, an English diabolist seeking Hetep's favour

stages.title: Fate Lends a Hand
stages.clues: A cart reaches Wormhout: Iain the Scot wounded, with his wife Eleanor, son Donncadh and daughter-in-law Mari. Donncadh, consors of Vindolanda, invokes the treaty of 886 before Markus and Cornelius, who send the characters.
stages.stopped: The magi accept. Donncadh tells of the raid and of one stolen black stone engraved with magic, and no more. He holds an Arcane Connection to his daughter; an Intellego Corpus spell of level 10 gives her direction, or whether she lives, and takes him half an hour.

stages.title: De Panne
stages.clues: Smoke still rises from Iain's house. Dockworkers saw an English ship leave at night, soon after the fire. At the Red Lion they heard talk of Exeter.
stages.stopped: Iain's ship is still in port and Donncadh takes it.

stages.title: Exeter
stages.clues: Two days' sail up the Exe. Iain's sailors know the ship that fled. Quiet money gets the name of Lord Peter.
stages.stopped: They get directions to his manor.

stages.title: Lord Peter's Manor
stages.clues: The magician has rebuilt the gateway and forced Brighde to open it. Six guards remain, and the servants are locked in.
stages.stopped: Donncadh opens the gate, and may have to explain where it leads.

stages.title: Scartaris Sanctum
stages.clues: Two dozen corpses and broken gargoyles fill the first chamber. In Victor's laboratory two interlocked circles hold domes of ice: a tall man in Roman robes and a squatting dog-like thing, frozen, joined by silver ribbons from their eyes. Brighde is tied to a chair and Lord Peter is at a ritual over the demon's ward, which cracks when he is interrupted.
stages.ignored: Fighting Lord Peter and Whisper, the characters see the host body shatter and the ribbons strike Brighde. Hetep takes her, shifts her to his beast shape, attacks Donncadh once and flees down a hidden tunnel that collapses behind him. Victor's ribbons strike a magus, Penetration 50 + stress die, and the first to fail falls in a fit, carrying him as a ghost.

stages.title: Victor Offers a Deal
stages.clues: Victor puts the magi to sleep (as Rego Mentem 25, Penetration +50) and meets them in his Morphean Landscape, at a round marble table with armed men of about 870 along the walls. He offers full membership and answers briefly: he made no pact, and sought Damhan-Allaidh or his soulstone.
stages.stopped: They swear the oath and wake. His host is led to a grimoire of tunnelling spells, and they clear the tunnel in about 12 hours, coming out halfway up Snaefell's southern slope.

stages.title: Snaefellsnes
stages.clues: Farmsteads burn between them and the coast, and mutilated dead charge from one. Thord Sturluson rides up with thirty men; bravery and an offer to hunt the creature win him. Over twenty Icelanders and thirty Norwegians are dead.
stages.stopped: Thord says the demon killed a Norwegian crew and put out to sea with them, and he has another vessel.

stages.title: Ocean Chase
stages.clues: Hetep has about four hours' start, but his dead sail badly. The Arcane Connection to Brighde still works with Intellego Animal for her shape, until he notices and blocks it; replaced planking of his ship is a connection too.
stages.stopped: Board the ghost-ship and bring Victor's host to arm's length. Hetep may strike once before Victor passes into him; Brighde reverts and lies in a coma for about a day. Thord and his men are deeply impressed.

stages.title: What Now?
stages.clues: Both ships sail back to Snaefellsnes, and Thord wants a tale the public will accept: monsters are not unknown, nor are magicians hunting them. A service of thanks at the church on his estate at Stad is followed by a feast.
stages.stopped: Brighde can open the gate back to the manor if her father is dead, and the gatestone goes home to De Panne. Devon will not miss Lord Peter, and De Panne's burghers will back the magi.

stages.title: Registered in Normandy
stages.clues: Wormhout now knows that Vindolanda survives, and the Quaesitor Iphimedeia comes to investigate. Iain and Victor, wary of the wider Order knowing their affairs, must reassure her.
stages.stopped: She agrees to register Vindolanda as a covenant of the Normandy Tribunal. Redcaps deliver to and collect from Iain's house in De Panne, forbidden to tell other magi where it is, and Wormhout stays an ally (p. 75).

neighbours.secrets:
The saga's opening adventure, of 1220 (ch. 9). During Pralix's war Hetep maimed Iain's Gift. He kept his External Soul, joined Vindolanda as a full magus, and hid with the Scartaris gatestone in 888. He searched the world for centuries, learned Natural Magic, grew rich as a merchant, and settled in De Panne in 1182, where he married. In 1219 he gave up on Victor and went to ask Cad Gadu for aid, was turned away for lack of an invitation, and a diabolist followed him home (p. 77).

The oath the magi swear and the charter are on the covenant of Vindolanda's record (p. 85). Donncadh and Brighde are both Gifted and may become player characters; Donncadh could stay a Mythic Companion (p. 87).

neighbours.name: The Dragon's Bane
neighbours.summary: Sir Ivain of De Panne has found a dragon's prophecy that his town will burn, and is taking ship for Iceland with his holy sword to kill the dragon first. The magi are welcome aboard.
neighbours.secrets:
A way to bring characters to Iceland without Spider in the Ice (p. 63). Pan Caudarax promised to raze the town for a past slight; the prophecy is on p. 140. Magi may want the vis of the corpse, or to guard Ivain.

Their presence on the ship may be enough to rouse the Guardians (p. 7). Local magicians can tell them of the dragon's weak spot if they enlist them. Faced, Pan Caudarax asks why the knight defends thieves. He will destroy De Panne only when his hoard there is robbed; once Ivain understands, he withdraws his challenge and goes home.

neighbours.name: An Eye on the North
neighbours.summary: Word of Iceland's Galdramen Hreppar reaches the Order, which is intrigued, alarmed or both, and young magi are chosen to go and see.

details.antagonist: The Order's fear of the Order of Odin

neighbours.secrets: Heorot on Zealand (see Ultima Thule) was founded partly to watch the Order of Odin, and the Hreppar may be the nearest thing to it outside tales. The trip may be a spying mission with the quaesitores' approval, or a diplomatic one, as the characters' skills suit (pp. 63-64).

neighbours.name: The Toframanna Saga
neighbours.summary: A saga of foreign magicians, whom Icelanders call toframenn, learning to live in a land of neighbours.
neighbours.secrets:
Toframan, feminine tofrakona, is the Icelandic magicians' word for foreign magicians, whose power rests on no song, giant blood, runes or herbs, so the saga is the saga of the magi (p. 62).

Land and weather (p. 62). Volcanic ground everywhere; rugged lowlands, and an interior of trolls, giants and violent spirits that bleakly offsets the summer meadows. Stick to the paths and the ponies. A day seldom passes without rain, sleet, hail or snow, above all in the west, and sun often follows.

Society (pp. 62-63). Everyone of rank knows everyone, and writes; even labourers follow the intrigues. Foreign magicians are endlessly discussed, and a magical attempt at privacy makes it worse. Secret crimes come out, for Icelanders despise those who disown their acts. Bread and ale are luxuries and a storgodi is a simple farmer, yet the freemen are proud: tenant farmers expect to be heard, abuse brings vengeance or a lawsuit, and reputations are national. If Mythic Iceland follows history the storgodi's feudal schemes fail and the Norwegian king must treat with the farmers themselves.

Premises of the saga (pp. 68-69). High fantasy, with the characters as heroes. A mature Order: expansion is over, and Join or Die on the borders is a sport. The Oath is applied pragmatically, and quaesitores act when the Order is endangered. Commoners do not know of the Order; Jerbiton envoys keep the peace with Church and courts. Open magic breaks no Code but angers churchmen. Magi swear no feudal oath and strike deals with lords, but being in thing with a godi carries no feudal duty, as the characters may have to argue at Tribunal. Young magi expect hard terms from a covenant, and take them.

Virtues and Flaws to refuse (p. 74): Quaesitor, Hedge Wizard, Infamous Master, Tormenting Master, Discredited Lineage, since the covenant is isolated; Secret Vis Source and Vis Obligation, since vis is scarce and shared.

The feud is the theme: Order against Damhan-Allaidh, Einar against the dragon, and behind them the storgodi's mundane feud (pp. 18-19, 67). The arcs are linear in places, and meant to be left to the storyguide's nudging or dropped (p. 68).

neighbours.name: Vindolanda
neighbours.summary: The holdings of the covenant of Vindolanda, in sites far apart. It keeps no single home that a stranger could visit.
neighbours.secrets:
The covenant's main site in Northumberland never held a sanctum: each magus's sanctum lay elsewhere, joined to it by a Gatestone. None of those gates works now except the one into Scartaris, which Lord Peter stole from De Panne (p. 88). The aura here is that of Scartaris, the only site in use.

The Northumbrian site is rubble in an Infernal aura; Macomb's sanctum has collapsed; Ealasaid's is partly flooded and full of sea life. The gateways to both lie buried in the wreck of the main site, and the gatestone to the Temple valley is in Ealasaid's sanctum. As the saga is written, the magi find these only after Brighde's Gauntlet (p. 88).

The book's saga adds neither Liam's sanctum nor Iain's original one, and leaves a storyguide free to invent these or any others. Being gruagachan, neither man needed a laboratory (p. 96).

neighbours.name: Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A hidden sanctum of the covenant of Vindolanda.
neighbours.secrets:
The first sanctum Vindolanda made, deep inside the southern peak of Snaefell, in a +5 magical aura. The volcano stands just over 1440 paces high near the tip of the Snaefellsnes peninsula, which runs some forty miles into the Atlantic; it can be seen a hundred miles off, and two main peaks stand north and south of its crater (pp. 88-89).

When the Carnac gateway opened, the magi found the Temple valley and then Iceland, and learned how rich the island was in vis. The temple was plainly tied to Damhan-Allaidh, so it was unsafe. Scartaris gave easy access to the vis in a place he did not know (p. 88).

There are only two laboratory areas, both taken by the elders Victor and Iain, and quarters for a handful of covenfolk. There is no vis supply, no servants but those the magi bring, and a library with only the basics on the Arts (p. 88). New magi must carve their own space from the mountain with the library's spells (p. 90).

Magic items run the sanctum; most were bought from House Verditius with the vis found when Iceland was first explored, and a single tome in the library sets out how each works (p. 90). The brazier in the Gate Room gives light like sun through cloud to every room but the sancta, sleeping chambers and library, through window-like shapes in the ceilings; an Imaginem requisite shows open sky in them. It runs on unattended or may be switched twenty-four times a day. Its Creo and Perdo also hold the main rooms at one temperature, set by touch and concentration (p. 91). Sancta, library, private chambers and servants' quarters each have an item giving a strange shadowless light, switched twenty-four times a day (p. 91). Each room of the baths has a heating or cooling item set by touch and concentration, and all start inactive (p. 91). Lead-lined channels carry the bath water, and lead-lined drains take the overflow to a big bronze vat whose Perdo effect destroys everything inanimate but metal and gems (p. 91). A Structure version of Chamber of Spring Breezes keeps the air fresh (p. 91).

The whole peninsula is full of trolls, enemies of the covenant (p. 89; their statistics are on p. 30).

neighbours.name: Gate Room, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: A chamber thirty paces square whose high vault rests on twelve pillar arches, each pillar carrying a perch made for a gargoyle; mosaics cover floor and walls. The gate from De Panne stands in an alcove in the south wall; two corridors run west and one north. In the southeast corner sits the brazier that lights and warms most of the sanctum (pp. 89, 91).

neighbours.name: Laundry Room, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Twelve paces by ten. Stone basins along one wall run with warm water when working; a magical rack on the other wall dries any wet inanimate thing within a minute, by a Perdo Aquam effect (pp. 89, 91).

neighbours.name: Meeting Hall, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Twelve paces by seventeen, empty, and made impressive by the finely decorated ceiling (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Kitchen, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Twelve paces by six and well equipped. A big magical oven stands by the west wall, its heat set by a user's concentration. The fountain here is Scartaris's drinking water: it draws and purifies water from a deep shaft into a glacial fissure, as often as wished and for as long as the user concentrates. A wooden partition enchanted against putrefaction closes off the larder (pp. 89, 91).

neighbours.name: Latrine, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Eight paces by six, with stone benches on the north and south walls whose holes open on the drainage that destroys inanimate matter (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Servants' Quarters, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Twelve paces by eight, divided into four sleeping closets (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Store Rooms, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Two small rooms beside the laundry room, printed only on the map (p. 90).

neighbours.name: Library, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Twelve paces by ten, with four lecterns and four writing desks. About fifty books stand on their own lecterns along the walls, with room for ten times as many, and an enchantment preserves them. Iain's accounts and ledgers lie among them; the book promises details that it never gives (pp. 89, 91-92).

neighbours.name: Victor's Private Chambers, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Lectern, writing desk, bed, chests and cabinets, with Victor's sanctum marker on the door (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Victor's Lab, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Victor's body remains within the ward in the western corner. The laboratory is equipped but holds no consumables, and a season's work would make it usable. His sanctum marker is on the door (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Iain's Private Chambers, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Lectern, writing desk, bed, chests and cabinets, with signs of only occasional use, and Iain's sanctum marker on the door. A strongbox by the bed holds 500 pounds of silver; a box under the bed holds a pair of unused gatestones (pp. 89-90).

neighbours.name: Iain's Lab, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Equipped for a Natural Magician, with Iain's sanctum marker on the door (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Weapons Yard, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: Forty paces by ten, where Vindolanda's grogs once trained. The training gear left here is too brittle with age to use (p. 90).

neighbours.name: Secret Tunnel, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: The way out: two miles of stairs ending on the southern slope of Snaefell about 500 paces above the sea. Victor dug it as an exploration tunnel, climbing nearly a thousand paces. Its mouth is well hidden and unremarkable, about three miles from the nearest farmstead (pp. 89-90).

neighbours.name: The Baths, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: The bathing rooms of the Scartaris sanctum.
neighbours.secrets: The baths are dry and their items inactive (p. 92). To restore them, learn each item's activation, then balance heat and flow carefully. Brought up step by step from modest settings, all is well. Turned on at full power, the caldaria do +5 damage a round, the laconicum +10, and the frigidarium freezes and floods. Full working order takes about a month, then about an hour a week of adjustments, at least two full-time attendants (more with heavy use), and a season of a mason's repairs every five years.

neighbours.name: Apodyterium, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the baths of Scartaris.
neighbours.secrets: The changing room (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Tepidarium, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the baths of Scartaris.
neighbours.secrets: The warm room, warm but bearable when working (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Caldarium, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the baths of Scartaris.
neighbours.secrets: The hot room, steamy when working, with alcoves in its walls giving continuous plunges of hot water, hotter from one to the next (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Laconicum, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the baths of Scartaris.
neighbours.secrets: A round chamber of dry heat, set apart from the baths to stay dry; the higher the tier of seats, the greater the heat (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Frigidarium, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the baths of Scartaris.
neighbours.secrets: A round chamber full of cold water, which those leaving the laconicum should plunge straight into (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Great Bath, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the baths of Scartaris.
neighbours.secrets: A rectangular bath 22m by 8.8m and 1.5m deep, with pleasantly hot water flowing through and steps around its edges. Two big silver vessels half hidden in the chamber's western wall feed all the baths, one with steaming water, one tepid (pp. 90-91).

neighbours.name: Lucas Bath, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the baths of Scartaris.
neighbours.secrets: A tepid bath to cool the body before the return to the apodyterium (p. 90).

neighbours.name: Smaller Baths, Scartaris
neighbours.summary: A room of the baths of Scartaris.
neighbours.secrets: Three baths: one by the weapons yard for combatants to wash, one by the southern caldarium as fierce as that room, and one off the southern tepidarium, tolerably cold (p. 90).

neighbours.name: Old Vindolanda
neighbours.summary: The remains of one of the great Roman supply forts of Hadrian's Wall, halfway along it, about a mile northwest of the village of Bardon Mill in Northumberland. The site is hard to find, and those who look for it meet with accidents.

levels.name: Middle level
levels.notes:
Secrets
Infernally tainted Mentem vis is harvested here (p. 93).

levels.name: Top level
levels.notes:
Secrets
Ammon admits no magus here, and a spell must defeat his Might of 40. The gatestones lie under tons of rubble (pp. 93-94).

neighbours.secrets:
The covenant restored the fort to its full splendor and hid it from mundane notice with illusions and a kind of The Shrouded Glen. South of the wall, it still allied with Loch Leglean in the Praeses Septentrionalis. Damhan-Allaidh took it in 889, and a Hermetic army under Tremere and Flambeau magi then reduced it to rubble (p. 93).

Many innocent locals and covenfolk died in that attack. Damhan-Allaidh had penned them up to feed his sacrifices, and the Tremere and Flambeau leaders chose to leave no witnesses. His sacrifice and their murder both served Hell. The Shrouded Glen kept the dead from Christian burial, and every night their shades relive their end and beg for mercy. That stain overcame the magic aura, and an Infernal regio took its place (p. 93).

Finding the site takes a Perception stress roll of 12+ past the corrupted illusion and Shrouded Glen, and anyone trying will likely suffer an accident. Ammon, once Hetep's minion, rules the three-level regio with a score of infernal beasts (p. 93).

Infernally tainted Mentem vis can be harvested on the middle level: tiny white salt crystals, formed from the ghosts' tears, which the demon sends down to draw more magi; the book prints no amount. Magi distrust the source because the covenant that first claimed the site belonged to ill-fated Castrum Antiquum (Heirs to Merlin p. 15). Burnham holds the harvesting rights by a legal settlement, went once, read the history, and means to pass the site to the next naive young covenant it can steer into a swap (p. 93).

The gatestones lie on the top level under tons of rubble. Ammon bars magi from that level, so a spell must penetrate his Might to reach it. If the magi have followed Hetep here, the Sea Temple gatestone is already dug out and set up (pp. 93-94).
